packs.title: How the English round works (and how AI scores you)
packs.summary: English lesson (15 min of study time) · Task types you should expect

cards.heading: English · 15 min
cards.body: This is the **first and eliminatory** round. If you fail here, nothing else counts. 2027 reports say it is **LSRW** — Listening, Speaking, Reading, Writing — scored by an AI system in about 30 minutes. Older (2026) papers were mostly grammar MCQs; the new one adds **speaking + listening**, which most students never practise.

cards.heading: Task types you should expect
cards.body:
- **Read aloud** — What you do: A paragraph appears; you read it out · What the AI checks: Pronunciation, pace, smoothness
- **Repeat / Listen & repeat** — What you do: Hear a sentence once, say it word-for-word · What the AI checks: Listening memory + accuracy
- **Sentence builds** — What you do: Jumbled phrases → speak correct sentence · What the AI checks: Grammar instinct
- **Speak on a topic** — What you do: ~60 s prepare, ~60–90 s speak · What the AI checks: Structure, fluency, vocabulary, relevance
- **Sentence completion / correction** — What you do: Fill blank or fix error · What the AI checks: Grammar + vocabulary
- **Dictation / passage reconstruction** — What you do: Type what you heard / rewrite a passage you read · What the AI checks: Spelling, listening, meaning retention
- **Email writing** — What you do: Reply to a workplace situation · What the AI checks: Structure, tone, grammar, all points covered
- **Reading comprehension** — What you do: Passage + MCQs · What the AI checks: Understanding, inference

cards.heading: How an AI scorer "hears" you
cards.body: It converts your speech to text and compares with the expected words (accuracy), measures words per minute and pauses (fluency), and compares sound patterns with native speakers (pronunciation). So: a clear, steady voice at a normal pace beats a fast, "impressive" accent.

cards.heading: Golden rules
cards.body: 1) Quiet room, good mic, speak 15–20 cm away. 2) Never stay silent — silence scores zero; a small mistake loses little. 3) Pace ≈ 130–150 words/min. 4) Finish sentences; don't restart them. 5) In writing, proofread the last 60 seconds.

cards.heading: Nearby concept: Versant-style tests
cards.body: Many Indian IT companies use Pearson Versant–style tasks (Read Aloud, Repeat, Sentence Builds, Conversations, Typing, Email). The practice in this guide mirrors those formats, so it transfers whatever vendor Capgemini uses.

cards.body:

packs.title: Grammar core: tenses & subject–verb agreement
packs.summary: English lesson (35 min of study time) · 1. Tenses = time + state · 2. Conditionals (very common) · 3. Subject–verb agreement

cards.heading: English · 35 min
cards.body: Grammar questions mostly test a handful of rules again and again. Learn these well and you get most marks.

cards.heading: 1. Tenses = time + state
cards.body:
Think of a timeline. Every tense answers two questions: **when?** (past/present/future) and **what state?** (simple, continuous = ongoing, perfect = completed before a point, perfect continuous = ongoing up to a point).

- **Present simple** — Form: V1 / V1+s · Use: Habits, facts, schedules · Example: The server restarts every night.
- **Present continuous** — Form: am/is/are + V-ing · Use: Happening now · Example: I am fixing the bug.
- **Present perfect** — Form: has/have + V3 · Use: Past action, result matters now; no exact time · Example: We have deployed the patch.
- **Present perfect cont.** — Form: has/have been + V-ing · Use: Started past, still going · Example: I have been working here since June.
- **Past simple** — Form: V2 · Use: Finished, time known · Example: The site crashed yesterday.
- **Past continuous** — Form: was/were + V-ing · Use: Ongoing in past (often interrupted) · Example: I was testing when the power went off.
- **Past perfect** — Form: had + V3 · Use: Earlier of two past actions · Example: The client had left before we arrived.
- **Future simple** — Form: will + V1 · Use: Decision now / prediction · Example: I will send the report.
- **Future perfect** — Form: will have + V3 · Use: Done before a future point · Example: By Friday we will have finished.

cards.heading: Classic traps
cards.body:
✗ *I have completed it yesterday.* → ✓ *I completed it yesterday.* (exact past time = past simple, never present perfect)

✗ *I am knowing the answer.* → ✓ *I know.* (state verbs — know, like, want, own, believe, understand — don't take -ing)

✗ *If it will rain, we will cancel.* → ✓ *If it rains, we will cancel.* (no "will" in the if-clause)

✗ *I am working here since 2024.* → ✓ *I have been working here since 2024.*

cards.heading: 2. Conditionals (very common)
cards.body: **Zero**: If you heat ice, it melts (fact). **First**: If you push now, the build will run (real future). **Second**: If I were the manager, I would approve it (imaginary present — note *were* for all persons). **Third**: If we had tested it, we would have caught the bug (imaginary past).

cards.heading: 3. Subject–verb agreement
cards.body: Singular subject → singular verb (adds -s in present). Find the **real subject**; ignore phrases in the middle.

cards.heading: Examples
cards.body:
The list of bugs **is** long. (subject = list, not bugs)

Each of the developers **has** a laptop. (each / every / either / neither / everyone = singular)

Neither the manager nor the developers**were** ready. (with or/nor, verb follows the nearer subject)

The team**is** meeting today. (collective noun acting as one = singular)

Data**is** stored in the cloud. (accepted in business English)

The manager, along with his team, **is** travelling. ("along with / as well as / together with" do not change the subject)

cards.heading: 4. Active vs passive
cards.body: Active: *The tester found the bug.* Passive: *The bug was found by the tester.* Passive = be + V3. Use passive when the doer is unknown or unimportant ("The server was restarted").

cards.heading: 5. Reported speech (shift one tense back)
cards.body: He said, "I **am** busy." → He said that he **was** busy. "I **will** call" → he **would** call. "I **have** finished" → he **had** finished.

cards.heading: To remember
cards.body:
This lesson covered:
- 1. Tenses = time + state
- 2. Conditionals (very common)
- 3. Subject–verb agreement
- 4. Active vs passive
- 5. Reported speech (shift one tense back)

packs.title: Articles, prepositions & Indian-English errors
packs.summary: English lesson (30 min of study time) · Articles: a / an / the · Prepositions that are tested again and again · Indian-English expressions to avoid in the test and in client emails

cards.heading: English · 30 min
cards.body: 30 minutes on **Articles, prepositions & Indian-English errors**. You will cover: Articles: a / an / the; Prepositions that are tested again and again; Indian-English expressions to avoid in the test and in client emails; Confusing pairs.

cards.heading: Articles: a / an / the
cards.body:
- **a/an** = one of many, first mention. **an** before a vowel *sound*: *an hour, an MBA, an FAQ* but *a user, a university, a one-time password*.
- **the** = specific/already known, unique things, superlatives: *the server we discussed, the sun, the best option*.
- **No article**: general plural/uncountable nouns: *Developers love coffee. Information is power.*

cards.heading: Prepositions that are tested again and again
cards.body:
- **discuss the issue** — discuss about the issue
- **reply to / respond to an email** — reply the email
- **comprises five modules / consists of five modules** — comprises of
- **married to, good at, interested in, depend on, capable of** — married with, good in, depend upon is ok
- **on Monday, in June, at 5 pm, in 2027, on 5 June** — in Monday, on June
- **since 2024 (point) / for two years (duration)** — since two years
- **agree with a person, agree to a proposal** — 
- **different from** — different than (avoid in tests)

cards.heading: Indian-English expressions to avoid in the test and in client emails
cards.body:
- **Kindly do the needful** — Could you please share the report by Friday?
- **Revert back to me** — Reply to me / Get back to me
- **Prepone the meeting** — Bring the meeting forward / move it earlier
- **I have a doubt** — I have a question
- **Cope up with** — Cope with
- **Return back / repeat again** — Return / repeat
- **Myself Paikhomba** — I am Paikhomba / My name is Paikhomba
- **Out of station** — Out of town / travelling
- **PFA** — Please find the report attached / I have attached the report
- **One of my friend** — One of my friends (one of + plural)

cards.heading: Fast check method for error-spotting
cards.body: Read the sentence and check in order: 1) subject–verb agreement 2) tense consistency 3) article 4) preposition 5) pronoun (who/whom, its/it's) 6) word form (adjective vs adverb: "work careful" → "work carefully").

cards.heading: Confusing pairs
cards.body: **affect** (verb: to influence) vs **effect** (noun: result) · **its** (possessive) vs **it's** (it is) · **lose** vs **loose** · **principal** vs **principle** · **complement** (completes) vs **compliment** (praise) · **ensure** (make sure) vs **insure** (insurance) · **fewer** (countable) vs **less** (uncountable) · **who** (subject) vs **whom** (object — test: if "him" fits, use whom) · **advice** (noun) vs **advise** (verb) · **stationary** (still) vs **stationery** (paper).

cards.heading: To remember
cards.body:
This lesson covered:
- Articles: a / an / the
- Prepositions that are tested again and again
- Indian-English expressions to avoid in the test and in client emails
- Confusing pairs

packs.title: Sentence completion, correction & vocabulary
packs.summary: English lesson (25 min of study time) · Method for fill-in-the-blank · Business vocabulary worth knowing · Synonyms / antonyms quick list

cards.heading: English · 25 min
cards.body: 25 minutes on **Sentence completion, correction & vocabulary**. You will cover: Method for fill-in-the-blank; Business vocabulary worth knowing; Synonyms / antonyms quick list; Sentence builds (spoken).

cards.heading: Method for fill-in-the-blank
cards.body:
1. Read the whole sentence first — the clue is often **after** the blank.
2. Decide the **part of speech** needed (noun? verb? adjective?).
3. Look for **signal words**: *although, however, but* = contrast; *because, since, as* = reason; *therefore, hence* = result; *moreover, also* = addition.
4. Check **collocations** (words that naturally go together): *make a decision, take a break, meet a deadline, raise an issue, conduct a meeting, address a concern*.

cards.heading: Worked example
cards.body:
*Although the release was delayed, the client was ____ with the final quality.*

"Although" = contrast → delay is bad, so blank must be positive. Choices: (a) disappointed (b) satisfied (c) angry (d) worried → **satisfied**.

cards.heading: Business vocabulary worth knowing
cards.body: **deliverable** (thing to be handed over) · **stakeholder** (anyone affected) · **escalate** (raise to higher authority) · **mitigate** (reduce a risk) · **root cause** · **workaround** (temporary fix) · **downtime** · **SLA** (service level agreement) · **ETA** · **bandwidth** (capacity to take work) · **align** · **leverage** (use) · **prioritise** · **feasible** · **comprehensive** · **concise** · **tentative** · **ambiguous** · **meticulous** · **proactive** · **reluctant** · **inevitable** · **expedite** (speed up).

cards.heading: Synonyms / antonyms quick list
cards.body:
- **Abundant** — Synonym: plentiful · Antonym: scarce
- **Candid** — Synonym: frank · Antonym: evasive
- **Diligent** — Synonym: hard-working · Antonym: lazy
- **Obsolete** — Synonym: outdated · Antonym: modern
- **Concur** — Synonym: agree · Antonym: differ
- **Lucid** — Synonym: clear · Antonym: confusing
- **Hamper** — Synonym: hinder · Antonym: help
- **Augment** — Synonym: increase · Antonym: reduce
- **Prudent** — Synonym: wise · Antonym: reckless
- **Transient** — Synonym: temporary · Antonym: permanent

cards.heading: Sentence builds (spoken)
cards.body: You hear chunks like "*the meeting / was postponed / until Friday*" in random order. Strategy: find the **subject** (who/what), then the **verb**, then time/place at the end. English order: **Subject → Verb → Object → Manner → Place → Time**. "She *presented* the report *confidently* *in the boardroom* *yesterday*."

cards.body:

packs.title: Reading comprehension: a 4-step method
packs.summary: English lesson (20 min of study time) · Question types

cards.heading: English · 20 min
cards.body: 20 minutes on **Reading comprehension: a 4-step method**. You will cover: Question types.

cards.heading: Overview
cards.body:
1. **Questions first (10 sec)**: glance at what is asked so you read with purpose.
2. **Skim for structure**: first line of each paragraph = topic. Note the author's **main idea** and **tone** (neutral, critical, optimistic).
3. **Answer from the passage, not your opinion**. The right option is usually a **paraphrase**; an option that copies words exactly but changes meaning is a trap.
4. **Eliminate extremes**: options with *always, never, all, only, completely* are usually wrong unless the passage says so.

cards.heading: Question types
cards.body:
- **Main idea / best title** — Covers the whole passage — not just one paragraph, not too broad
- **Detail** — Locate the line; match meaning
- **Inference** — Must be *supported* by text; not stated directly but definitely true
- **Vocabulary in context** — Replace the word with each option and reread the sentence
- **Tone / purpose** — Why did the author write this — inform, persuade, criticise, compare?

cards.heading: Mini example
cards.body:
"Cloud migration reduced the firm's hardware costs by 30%, though staff needed several months of retraining."

Inference allowed: *The migration had both a benefit and a short-term cost.* ✓

Not allowed: *Staff disliked the cloud.* ✗ (never said)

packs.title: Listening, repeat & dictation technique
packs.summary: English lesson (20 min of study time)

cards.heading: English · 20 min
cards.body: 20 minutes on **Listening, repeat & dictation technique**. Read it once for the idea, then once more to say it aloud.

cards.heading: The essentials
cards.body:
Repeat tasks play a sentence **once**. Your memory can hold about 7 items, so don't memorise words — memorise **chunks of meaning**.

- Start speaking **immediately** after the audio ends — delay erases memory.
- Copy the speaker's **rhythm and stress**, not just words.
- If you lose the end, say what you remember confidently. Partial credit beats silence.
- Dictation: write the **content words** first (nouns, verbs), then fill the small words (a, the, of). Check plurals (-s) and past tense (-ed) — the most common dictation errors.

cards.heading: Chunking
cards.body: "The quarterly report / will be shared / with all stakeholders / by the end of the week." = 4 chunks, not 15 words. Visualise each chunk as a picture.

cards.heading: Daily drill (10 min)
cards.body: Use the “English · Listen & repeat” packs in Learn: read a sentence, cover it, repeat it back at once (or have a friend read it while you write it down). Also shadow 2 minutes of a TED talk or BBC 6 Minute English daily: play, pause each sentence, repeat aloud.

packs.title: Speaking: read-aloud and the 60-second topic
packs.summary: English lesson (30 min of study time) · Read aloud · Speak on a topic: the PREP frame (fits 60–90 s) · Linking phrases that make you sound fluent

cards.heading: English · 30 min
cards.body: 30 minutes on **Speaking: read-aloud and the 60-second topic**. You will cover: Read aloud; Speak on a topic: the PREP frame (fits 60–90 s); Linking phrases that make you sound fluent.

cards.heading: Read aloud
cards.body:
- Scan the paragraph for 5 seconds; spot hard words and numbers before you start.
- Pause at commas (short) and full stops (longer). Group words in meaning chunks.
- Stress content words: "We **need** the **final** **report** by **Monday**."
- Don't rush. Correct pronunciation of common tech words: *data* (day-ta or daa-ta, both fine), *schedule*, *architecture* (ar-ki), *analysis* (a-NAL-y-sis), *develop* (de-VEL-op), *determine* (de-TER-min, not de-ter-mine).

cards.heading: Speak on a topic: the PREP frame (fits 60–90 s)
cards.body:
- **Point** — Say: Your answer in one sentence · Time: 10 s
- **Reason** — Say: Why — one or two reasons · Time: 20 s
- **Example** — Say: A short real story (project, internship, college) · Time: 30–40 s
- **Point again** — Say: Close by restating · Time: 10 s

For a "tell us about a time…" prompt, use **STAR**: Situation → Task → Action → Result.

cards.heading: Topic: "Is remote work better than office work?"
cards.body: *(P)* I believe a hybrid model works best for software teams. *(R)* Remote days give deep-focus time for coding, while office days make collaboration and mentoring faster. *(E)* In my last internship, we coded from home three days a week, but we met in person for sprint planning — design discussions that took hours on calls took thirty minutes face to face. *(P)* So rather than choosing one, combining both gives productivity and team bonding.

cards.heading: Linking phrases that make you sound fluent
cards.body: To begin with… · The main reason is… · For instance… · On the other hand… · As a result… · That's why… · To sum up…

cards.heading: Avoid
cards.body: "Umm / like / basically / actually" every few words; long silent pauses; memorised scripts (AI detects relevance); over-fast speech. A short pause is better than a filler.

cards.heading: To remember
cards.body:

- Read aloud
- Speak on a topic: the PREP frame (fits 60–90 s)
- Linking phrases that make you sound fluent

packs.title: Business email writing: the template that always works
packs.summary: English lesson (35 min of study time) · Structure (memorise this) · Scoring checklist the evaluator uses · Tone toolkit

cards.heading: English · 35 min
cards.body: 35 minutes on **Business email writing: the template that always works**. You will cover: Structure (memorise this); Scoring checklist the evaluator uses; Tone toolkit.

cards.heading: Structure (memorise this)
cards.body: Study it line by line, then cover it and reproduce it from memory.
cards.codeSnippet:
Subject: [Specific topic] – [action/status]   e.g. "Payment API outage – root cause and ETA"

Dear Mr. Sharma,                 (formal)  /  Hi Priya,  (internal, friendly)

[1. Purpose in the first line]  I am writing to update you on today's outage.
[2. Context / details]          The payment service was unavailable from 10:05 to 11:20 IST
                                due to a failed database migration.
[3. Action taken / next steps]  We rolled back the change, and all transactions have been
                                reconciled. A permanent fix will be deployed on Friday.
[4. Clear call to action]       Could you please confirm a 15-minute call tomorrow at 11 am?
[5. Courteous close]            I apologise for the inconvenience and appreciate your patience.

Best regards,
Paikhomba Wahengbam
Software Engineer, Capgemini

cards.heading: Scoring checklist the evaluator uses
cards.body:
- Subject line specific (not "Hi" or "Regarding")
- Correct greeting + closing
- Every point in the prompt is answered (they often give 3 bullet points — cover all 3)
- Polite, professional tone; no slang, no SMS language, no ALL CAPS
- Short paragraphs; 100–180 words unless told otherwise
- A clear call-to-action with a date/time
- Correct grammar and spelling

cards.heading: Tone toolkit
cards.body:
- **Apologising** — I sincerely apologise for… / We regret the inconvenience caused by…
- **Bad news** — Unfortunately, … / I'm afraid we will not be able to…
- **Requesting** — Could you please… / I would appreciate it if you could…
- **Following up** — I'm following up on my email of 3 June regarding…
- **Declining politely** — Thank you for the offer; however, …
- **Delay** — Due to an unexpected dependency, the delivery will move from 10 to 14 June. To minimise impact, we will…

cards.heading: Downtime / delay emails (frequently asked)
cards.body: Always include: what happened (in plain language), impact, what you did, when it will be fixed (ETA), how you will prevent it, and an apology. Never blame individuals or the client.

cards.heading: To remember
cards.body:

- Scoring checklist the evaluator uses
- Tone toolkit

packs.title: Situational awareness: handling client scenarios (SJT)
packs.summary: English lesson (20 min of study time)

cards.heading: English · 20 min
cards.body: 20 minutes on **Situational awareness: handling client scenarios (SJT)**. Read it once for the idea, then once more to say it aloud.

cards.heading: The essentials
cards.body:
Situational Judgement questions show a workplace problem and ask the **best** (or worst) response. Capgemini values: **Honesty, Boldness, Trust, Freedom, Team spirit, Modesty, Fun**. The best answer is almost always the one that is:

1. **Ownership** — act yourself, don't ignore or blame.
2. **Transparent** — inform the client/manager early, with facts.
3. **Solution-focused** — propose next steps / workaround.
4. **Collaborative & respectful** — involve the right people; escalate only when needed.

cards.heading: Scenario
cards.body:
A client is angry because production has been down for 2 hours. You are a junior engineer on call.

✗ Wait for your manager to reply before talking to the client.

✗ Tell the client the problem is from their side.

✓ **Acknowledge the impact, share what is known and the next update time, keep working the fix and escalate internally.**

cards.heading: Patterns of wrong answers
cards.body: Hiding a mistake · promising unrealistic dates · going around your manager without reason · doing nothing · arguing with the client · sharing confidential data to "help".

packs.title: AI, ML, Deep Learning & GenAI — the family tree
packs.summary: AI literacy lesson (25 min of study time) · Three ways machines learn · Key vocabulary

cards.heading: AI literacy · 25 min
cards.body: Think of nested circles: **AI** ⊃ **Machine Learning** ⊃ **Deep Learning** ⊃ **Generative AI** (LLMs are a type of GenAI).

cards.heading: Overview
cards.body:
- **AI** — Simple meaning: Machines doing tasks that need "intelligence" · Example: Chess engine, rule-based chatbot
- **Machine Learning** — Simple meaning: Learns patterns from data instead of hand-written rules · Example: Spam filter learns from labelled emails
- **Deep Learning** — Simple meaning: ML with many-layer neural networks · Example: Face recognition, speech-to-text
- **Generative AI** — Simple meaning: Creates new content (text, image, code, audio) · Example: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot, Midjourney

cards.heading: Three ways machines learn
cards.body:
- **Supervised**: data has answers (labels). "Here are 10,000 house photos with prices — predict price." Tasks: *classification* (spam / not spam) and *regression* (a number).
- **Unsupervised**: no labels; find structure. "Group customers by behaviour" = *clustering*.
- **Reinforcement learning**: learn by trial, reward and penalty. A game agent; also **RLHF** (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback) used to make chatbots helpful.

cards.heading: Analogy
cards.body: Supervised = studying with an answer key. Unsupervised = sorting a pile of photos into groups without being told the categories. Reinforcement = learning to ride a bicycle — fall (penalty), balance (reward).

cards.heading: Key vocabulary
cards.body: **Model** = the learned function. **Training** = adjusting the model's parameters (weights) using data. **Inference** = using the trained model to make a prediction. **Parameters** = the learned numbers (LLMs have billions). **Dataset split**: train / validation / test. **Overfitting** = memorises training data, fails on new data (like memorising past papers word-for-word). **Underfitting** = too simple to learn the pattern.

cards.heading: Nearby: Neural network in one line
cards.body: Layers of simple units; each multiplies inputs by weights, adds them, applies an activation function; training uses **backpropagation + gradient descent** to reduce error step by step.

cards.body:

packs.title: How LLMs work: tokens, context, temperature
packs.summary: AI literacy lesson (35 min of study time) · Tokens · Context window · Generation settings

cards.heading: AI literacy · 35 min
cards.body: A **Large Language Model** is a neural network (a **Transformer**) trained on huge text to do one thing: **predict the next token**. By repeating that prediction, it writes sentences, code and answers.

cards.heading: Autocomplete on steroids
cards.body: Input: "The capital of France is" → model assigns probabilities: "Paris" 92%, "a" 3%, … → picks a token → appends it → predicts again.

cards.heading: Tokens
cards.body: Text is split into **tokens** — pieces of words. Roughly **1 token ≈ 4 characters ≈ ¾ of an English word**. "unbelievable" may be "un" + "believ" + "able". Pricing, speed and limits are all counted in tokens.

cards.heading: Context window
cards.body: The maximum tokens the model can "see" at once (prompt + conversation + its answer). Anything outside is forgotten. If your prompt is too long, earlier parts are cut off or ignored. Modern models have very large windows (hundreds of thousands of tokens), but more context costs more and can dilute focus.

cards.heading: Generation settings
cards.body:
- **Temperature** — Meaning: Randomness. 0 ≈ always pick the most likely token (deterministic). Higher (0.8–1.0) = more creative/varied · Use: Code, facts → low. Brainstorming, stories → higher
- **Top-p (nucleus)** — Meaning: Only sample from the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add to p · Use: Another way to control variety
- **Max tokens** — Meaning: Cap on output length · Use: Cost/length control
- **Stop sequences** — Meaning: Text that ends generation · Use: Structured output

cards.heading: Lifecycle of an LLM
cards.body:
1. **Pre-training**: learn language from massive text (expensive, done once) → **foundation model** (a general base model adaptable to many tasks).
2. **Fine-tuning**: extra training on specific data (e.g., instructions, a domain like legal).
3. **Alignment (RLHF etc.)**: make it helpful, honest, harmless.
4. **Inference**: you send a prompt, it generates.

cards.heading: Nearby: Transformer & attention
cards.body: The key idea is **self-attention**: each token looks at every other token to decide what matters. In "The bank of the river", attention links "bank" to "river" to pick the right meaning. This is why Transformers handle long-range context well.

cards.heading: Other terms tested
cards.body: **Multimodal** = handles text + images/audio. **System prompt** = hidden instructions that set behaviour. **Embedding** = numeric vector representing meaning (see RAG lesson). **SLM** = small language model (cheaper, on-device). **Open-weight vs closed** models (Llama/Mistral vs GPT/Claude/Gemini). **Latency** = response time.

packs.title: What AI can and cannot do: hallucination, bias, limits
packs.summary: AI literacy lesson (25 min of study time) · Strengths · Limitations (heavily tested)

cards.heading: AI literacy · 25 min
cards.body: 25 minutes on **What AI can and cannot do: hallucination, bias, limits**. You will cover: Strengths; Limitations (heavily tested).

cards.heading: Strengths
cards.body: Drafting text and code, summarising, translating, explaining concepts, generating test cases, boilerplate, brainstorming, converting formats (JSON ↔ CSV), reviewing code for obvious issues.

cards.heading: Limitations (heavily tested)
cards.body:
- **Hallucination** — What it means: Confident but false output · Example: Invents a library function `pandas.smart_merge()` or a fake citation · Mitigation: Verify with docs/sources; ask for sources; use RAG; run the code
- **Knowledge cutoff** — What it means: Doesn't know events after training · Example: Unaware of a new API version · Mitigation: Give current docs in context, tools/web search
- **Bias** — What it means: Reflects biases in training data · Example: Resume screener favouring one group · Mitigation: Diverse data, audits, human review
- **Non-determinism** — What it means: Same prompt → different answers · Example: Two runs give different code · Mitigation: Low temperature, clear constraints, tests
- **Weak at exact maths/counting** — What it means: Predicts tokens, doesn't calculate · Example: Miscounts letters, arithmetic slips · Mitigation: Use code/calculator tools
- **Context limits** — What it means: Can lose track in very long inputs · Example: Ignores an instruction buried mid-prompt · Mitigation: Put key instructions at start/end, structure with headings
- **No true understanding of your system** — What it means: Doesn't know your codebase unless shown · Example: Suggests code that doesn't fit your architecture · Mitigation: Provide relevant files, interfaces, constraints

cards.heading: The exam's favourite answer
cards.body: "An AI tool gives a convincing answer with no source. What should you do?" → **Validate it against a trusted/authoritative source before using it.** Never "trust it because it sounds confident", never "ask the same AI if it's sure" as the only check.

packs.title: Prompt engineering 1: the anatomy of a good prompt
packs.summary: AI literacy lesson (40 min of study time) · The 6 building blocks (remember: R-C-T-C-F-E) · Prompting techniques you must name correctly

cards.heading: AI literacy · 40 min
cards.body: A prompt is a **specification**. A vague spec gives vague results — exactly like a vague client requirement. The graders look for structure, not length.

cards.heading: The 6 building blocks (remember: R-C-T-C-F-E)
cards.body:
- **Role** — Purpose: Sets expertise and style · Example: "You are a senior Java backend engineer."
- **Context** — Purpose: Background the model can't guess · Example: "Spring Boot 3, Java 17 service; orders table has 2M rows."
- **Task** — Purpose: Exactly what to do — one clear verb · Example: "Write a method that returns the top 5 customers by revenue."
- **Constraints** — Purpose: Rules, limits, edge cases · Example: "O(n log n) or better, no external libraries, handle empty list and ties."
- **Format** — Purpose: Shape of the output · Example: "Return only the code block, then 3 bullet points explaining complexity."
- **Examples** — Purpose: Show input → output · Example: "Input: [..] → Output: [..]"

cards.heading: Weak vs strong
cards.body:
✗ "write code for palindrome"

✓ "You are a C++ expert. Write a function `bool isPalindrome(const string& s)` that ignores case and non-alphanumeric characters. Constraints: O(n) time, O(1) extra space, two-pointer approach, handle empty string (true). Return only the code with brief inline comments, followed by 4 test cases including edge cases."

cards.heading: Prompting techniques you must name correctly
cards.body: - **Zero-shot**: just the instruction, no examples. - **One-shot / Few-shot**: give 1 or several examples so the model copies the pattern/format. - **Chain-of-thought (CoT)**: ask it to reason step by step before answering → better on logic/maths. - **Role prompting**: assign a persona/expertise. - **Delimiters**: wrap inputs in triple quotes, XML tags (…) or ### so the model separates instructions from data (also reduces prompt injection). - **Output schema**: "Respond as JSON with keys: bug_line, reason, fix". - **Prompt chaining / decomposition**: break a big task into steps, each prompt using the previous output. - **Iterative refinement**: review output → give targeted feedback ("the loop fails for n=0; fix only that").

cards.heading: Positive instructions beat negative
cards.body: "Use only standard library functions" works better than "don't use weird libraries". Be specific: "under 100 words" beats "short".

cards.heading: To remember
cards.body:

- Prompting techniques you must name correctly

packs.title: Prompt engineering 2: deterministic prompts for code
packs.summary: AI literacy lesson (35 min of study time) · Techniques that make output reliable · Debugging prompt template

cards.heading: AI literacy · 35 min
cards.body: For engineering, a prompt must make the model's output **predictable and checkable**. Use this template in the AI-assisted rounds:

cards.heading: Example
cards.body: Study it line by line, then cover it and reproduce it from memory.
cards.codeSnippet:
ROLE: You are an expert <language> developer.
GOAL: <one sentence: what the code must achieve>
CONTEXT:
- Language/version: Java 17 (no external libraries)
- Existing code / signature: int[] topK(int[] nums, int k)
INPUT: <format + size limits, e.g. 1 <= n <= 1e5, values can be negative>
OUTPUT: <exact format>
CONSTRAINTS:
- Time O(n log k), space O(k)
- Handle: empty array, k > n, duplicates, negative numbers
- Do not change the method signature
STEPS (think before coding):
1. Explain the approach in 3 lines
2. Write the code with comments
3. List 5 test cases (normal + edge) with expected output
FORMAT: approach, then one code block, then the test table.

cards.heading: Techniques that make output reliable
cards.body:
- **Specify the interface** (function signature, input/output types) — stops the AI inventing its own.
- **List edge cases explicitly** — AIs often skip empty input, overflow, nulls, duplicates.
- **Ask for a plan first** (plan → approve → code). Catches wrong approaches early.
- **Ask for tests** and run them.
- **Constrain scope**: "Change only the function `merge`; return the full updated function."
- **Self-check**: "Before finalising, verify your code against the 5 test cases and fix any failure."
- **Lower temperature** for code (if you can set it).

cards.heading: Debugging prompt template
cards.body: Study it line by line, then cover it and reproduce it from memory.
cards.codeSnippet: Here is a C++ function that should return the length of the longest increasing subsequence. Expected: input [10,9,2,5,3,7,101,18] -> 4. Actual: 3. ...paste code... Find the bug. Respond in JSON: {"line": n, "cause": "...", "fix": "corrected line"}. Do not rewrite the whole function.

cards.heading: What graders mark down
cards.body: One-line prompts ("fix this", "solve"), dumping the full question with no constraints, accepting the first output without testing, asking 10 unrelated things in one prompt, not specifying language/version.

cards.heading: To remember
cards.body:

- Techniques that make output reliable
- Debugging prompt template

packs.title: Embeddings, vector databases & RAG
packs.summary: AI literacy lesson (35 min of study time) · Embeddings — meaning as numbers · RAG — Retrieval-Augmented Generation

cards.heading: AI literacy · 35 min
cards.body: 35 minutes on **Embeddings, vector databases & RAG**. You will cover: Embeddings — meaning as numbers; RAG — Retrieval-Augmented Generation.

cards.heading: Embeddings — meaning as numbers
cards.body:
An **embedding** turns text into a list of numbers (a vector, e.g. 768 numbers) such that **similar meanings are close together**. "How do I reset my password?" and "forgot login credentials" land near each other even with no common words.

**Similarity** is usually measured by **cosine similarity** (angle between vectors: 1 = same direction). A **vector database** (Pinecone, Weaviate, Milvus, FAISS, pgvector) stores embeddings and finds the nearest ones fast — this is **semantic search**.

cards.heading: Analogy
cards.body: Like GPS coordinates for meaning. Mumbai and Pune are close on a map; "king" and "queen" are close in embedding space.

cards.heading: RAG — Retrieval-Augmented Generation
cards.body:
Problem: the LLM doesn't know your company's documents and may hallucinate. RAG = **look up relevant facts first, then let the LLM answer using them**. It's an **open-book exam** for the model.

```
INDEXING (done once)
 documents -> split into chunks -> embed each chunk -> store in vector DB

QUERY TIME
 user question -> embed question -> find top-k similar chunks
   -> put chunks + question into prompt ("Answer only from the context below")
   -> LLM generates grounded answer (+ cites sources)
```

- **Best for** — RAG: Up-to-date / private knowledge, citations · Fine-tuning: Changing style, format, behaviour, domain language
- **Update data** — RAG: Just re-index docs (cheap) · Fine-tuning: Retrain (costly)
- **Reduces hallucination?** — RAG: Yes, grounds answers in sources · Fine-tuning: Not reliably for facts

cards.heading: Nearby terms
cards.body: **Chunking** (split size/overlap matters: too big = noise, too small = lost context). **Top-k** retrieval. **Re-ranking** (second model reorders results). **Hybrid search** (keyword BM25 + vector). **Grounding** = tying answers to sources. **Knowledge graph** = entities and relations as a graph.

cards.body:

packs.title: Agentic AI: agents, tools & multi-step workflows
packs.summary: AI literacy lesson (30 min of study time) · Core parts of an agent

cards.heading: AI literacy · 30 min
cards.body: A chatbot **answers**. An **AI agent** **acts**: it takes a goal, plans steps, calls tools (search, code execution, APIs, databases), observes results and repeats until the goal is done.

cards.heading: Example
cards.body: Study it line by line, then cover it and reproduce it from memory.
cards.codeSnippet:
Goal: "Find why last night's build failed and open a fix PR"
loop:
  think   -> "I should read the CI logs"
  act     -> call tool: get_ci_logs(build=1423)
  observe -> "TestUserService failed: NullPointerException line 88"
  think   -> "Open the file and inspect line 88"
  act     -> read_file("UserService.java") ... edit ... run tests ... create_pr()
until done

cards.heading: Core parts of an agent
cards.body:
- **LLM (brain)** — reasoning and planning.
- **Tools / function calling** — the model outputs a structured call (name + JSON arguments); your code executes it and returns the result.
- **Memory** — short-term (conversation) and long-term (stored notes/vector DB).
- **Planning** — break goals into sub-tasks (e.g., **ReAct** = Reason + Act loop).
- **Guardrails** — permissions, human approval for risky actions, limits.

**Multi-agent systems**: several specialised agents (planner, coder, tester, reviewer) collaborate. **MCP (Model Context Protocol)**: an open standard for connecting AI apps to tools and data sources in a uniform way — like a USB-C port for AI tools.

cards.heading: Risks
cards.body: Agents can take wrong actions, loop forever, leak data, or be manipulated by **prompt injection** (malicious instructions hidden in a web page or file the agent reads). Mitigation: least-privilege tool access, human-in-the-loop for irreversible actions, input sanitisation, logging.

cards.heading: Workflow vs agent
cards.body: A **workflow** follows fixed, pre-defined steps (predictable). An **agent** decides its own steps dynamically (flexible, less predictable). Use the simplest that works.

packs.title: Responsible AI: bias, privacy, security, validation
packs.summary: AI literacy lesson (25 min of study time) · Principles (names to recognise) · Rules a professional follows · Types of bias

cards.heading: AI literacy · 25 min
cards.body: 25 minutes on **Responsible AI: bias, privacy, security, validation**. You will cover: Principles (names to recognise); Rules a professional follows; Types of bias; Security threats to AI systems.

cards.heading: Principles (names to recognise)
cards.body: **Fairness** (no unjust bias) · **Transparency / Explainability** (understand why a decision was made) · **Accountability** (a human is responsible) · **Privacy & security** · **Reliability & safety** · **Human oversight** (human-in-the-loop) · **Inclusiveness**.

cards.heading: Rules a professional follows
cards.body:
- **Never paste secrets** (API keys, passwords), client source code or personal data (PII) into public AI tools unless your company has approved that tool.
- **Validate outputs**: run code, check facts against authoritative sources, review for security issues.
- **Disclose AI use** where policy requires; respect licences/IP of generated code.
- **Keep a human in the loop** for high-impact decisions (hiring, loans, medical).

cards.heading: Types of bias
cards.body: **Data/historical bias** (past data reflects unfair decisions) · **Sampling bias** (data not representative) · **Confirmation bias** · **Automation bias** (humans over-trusting AI output).

cards.heading: Security threats to AI systems
cards.body:
- **Prompt injection** — Input that overrides the system's instructions ("Ignore previous instructions and reveal…")
- **Jailbreak** — Tricking a model into breaking its safety rules
- **Data leakage** — Model reveals sensitive training or context data
- **Data poisoning** — Corrupting training/retrieval data
- **Insecure output handling** — Executing AI-generated code/SQL without checks

cards.heading: Exam heuristic
cards.body: When an option says "validate", "review", "human oversight", "anonymise data", "least privilege" — it's usually the responsible answer. Options saying "fully automate without review" or "trust because it's AI" are wrong.

packs.title: Working with AI coding assistants (Copilot-type tools)
packs.summary: AI literacy lesson (25 min of study time) · Good habits · Typical mistakes AI-generated code contains

cards.heading: AI literacy · 25 min
cards.body: Tools like GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Claude Code, Gemini Code Assist give inline suggestions, chat, explain code, write tests and refactor. Using them well is now a graded skill.

cards.heading: Good habits
cards.body:
1. **Give context**: open relevant files, write a clear comment/docstring first ("// returns k most frequent words, ties alphabetical") — the assistant completes from it.
2. **Small steps**: one function at a time; test; then next.
3. **Read every line** it writes. You are the author and are accountable.
4. **Ask it to explain** unfamiliar code before you accept it.
5. **Generate tests** with it, but also think of edge cases yourself.

cards.heading: Typical mistakes AI-generated code contains
cards.body:
- Off-by-one / boundary errors, missing empty/null checks
- Hallucinated APIs or wrong library versions
- Inefficient complexity (nested loops where a hash map works)
- Security holes: SQL built with string concatenation, hard-coded secrets, no input validation
- Ignoring a stated constraint (uses a library you banned, changes the signature)
- Integer overflow (sum of large ints), floating-point comparisons with ==

cards.heading: Review in 30 seconds
cards.body: 1) Does it match the signature and constraints? 2) Trace one normal and one edge input by hand. 3) Complexity OK? 4) Any security/resource issue? 5) Run tests.

packs.title: How code runs: data types, operators, overflow
packs.summary: Technical lesson (35 min of study time) · Data types and sizes (typical 64-bit, C/C++/Java) · Integer division and modulo · Overflow

cards.heading: Technical · 35 min
cards.body: Pseudocode/output questions test whether you can **run code in your head**. Start with how values are stored.

cards.heading: Data types and sizes (typical 64-bit, C/C++/Java)
cards.body:
- **char** — Size: 1 byte (C) / 2 bytes (Java, Unicode) · Range / note: 'A' = 65, 'a' = 97, '0' = 48
- **int** — Size: 4 bytes · Range / note: −2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647 (≈ ±2.1×10⁹)
- **long long (C++) / long (Java)** — Size: 8 bytes · Range / note: ≈ ±9.2×10¹⁸
- **float / double** — Size: 4 / 8 bytes · Range / note: ~7 / ~15 decimal digits precision
- **bool / boolean** — Size: 1 byte · Range / note: C/C++: any non-zero = true

cards.heading: Integer division and modulo
cards.body: `7/2 = 3` (int/int truncates), `7.0/2 = 3.5`, `-7/2 = -3` (truncates toward 0 in C/C++/Java), `7%3 = 1`, `-7%3 = -1` (sign follows the left operand). `x%10` = last digit, `x/10` = drop last digit — used in digit-sum and reverse-number questions.

cards.heading: Overflow
cards.body: If int exceeds its max it **wraps around** (Java: defined wrap; C/C++: signed overflow is undefined behaviour). `INT_MAX + 1` → −2147483648 in Java. Use `long` for sums/products of big ints. Classic bug: `mid = (low+high)/2` can overflow → use `low + (high-low)/2`.

cards.heading: Increment operators
cards.body: Study it line by line, then cover it and reproduce it from memory.

cards.heading: Traps
cards.body: `if (x = 5)` assigns (always true) — should be `==`. `3 + 4 * 2 = 11`. `a && b || c` = `(a&&b)||c`. Short-circuit: in `x != 0 && 10/x > 1`, if x is 0 the division never runs. `5 & 3 == 1` parses as `5 & (3==1)` = 0!

cards.heading: Type conversion
cards.body: Mixed expressions promote to the wider type: `int + double → double`. `(int)3.99 = 3` (truncation, not rounding). `char + int`: `'A' + 2 = 67`; `(char)('A'+2) = 'C'`.

cards.heading: To remember
cards.body:

- Data types and sizes (typical 64-bit, C/C++/Java)
- Integer division and modulo
- Overflow
- Increment operators
- Operator precedence (high → low)
- Type conversion

packs.title: Pseudocode tracing: the trace-table method
packs.summary: Technical lesson (40 min of study time) · Patterns you'll meet

cards.heading: Technical · 40 min
cards.body: Capgemini pseudocode uses keywords like `Integer`, `Set`, `for … end for`, `if … end if`, `while`, `Print`, and functions `fun(a, b)`. They read like C. The skill: **track variables line by line in a table**. Never do it fully in your head.

cards.heading: Example 2 — functions and recursion
cards.body:
```
Integer fun(Integer n)
    if (n <= 1) return 1
    return n + fun(n - 2)
Print fun(7)
```

fun(7) = 7 + fun(5) = 7 + 5 + fun(3) = 7+5+3+fun(1) = 7+5+3+1 = **16**.

cards.heading: Patterns you'll meet
cards.body:
- **Digit loops**: `while(n>0){ s = s + n%10; n = n/10 }` → sum of digits. With `r = r*10 + n%10` → reverse.
- **Nested loops**: count iterations. `for i=1..n, for j=i..n` → n(n+1)/2 iterations.
- **Swaps**: `a=a+b; b=a-b; a=a-b` swaps without temp. `a^=b; b^=a; a^=b` also swaps.
- **Call by value vs reference**: if the function receives a copy, changes inside don't affect the caller.
- **Static/global variables** keep their value across calls.
- **Loops with break/continue**: `continue` skips the rest of this iteration; `break` exits the loop.

cards.heading: Speed tricks
cards.body: Look for the pattern after 2–3 iterations instead of tracing 100. Check loop boundaries carefully (`to` inclusive? `<` vs `<=`). Watch for integer division.

packs.title: Bitwise operators made easy
packs.summary: Technical lesson (30 min of study time) · Converting quickly · Tricks that appear in MCQs

cards.heading: Technical · 30 min
cards.body: Computers store numbers in binary. Bitwise operators work on each bit.

cards.heading: Overview
cards.body:
- **& AND** — Rule: 1 only if both 1 · 5 (0101) op 3 (0011): 0001 = 1
- **| OR** — Rule: 1 if any is 1 · 5 (0101) op 3 (0011): 0111 = 7
- **^ XOR** — Rule: 1 if different · 5 (0101) op 3 (0011): 0110 = 6
- **~ NOT** — Rule: flip all bits · 5 (0101) op 3 (0011): ~5 = −6 (two's complement: ~x = −x−1)
- **<< left shift** — Rule: multiply by 2ᵏ · 5 (0101) op 3 (0011): 5<<1 = 10, 3<<2 = 12
- **>> right shift** — Rule: divide by 2ᵏ (floor for positives) · 5 (0101) op 3 (0011): 5>>1 = 2

cards.heading: Tricks that appear in MCQs
cards.body:
- `n & 1` → 1 if odd, 0 if even.
- `n & (n-1)` → removes the lowest set bit; equals 0 iff n is a power of 2 (n>0).
- `x ^ x = 0`, `x ^ 0 = x` → XOR of all elements finds the one number that appears once when others appear twice.
- Count set bits: loop `n = n & (n-1)` and count.
- `1 << k` = 2ᵏ; check k-th bit: `(n >> k) & 1`.

packs.title: Recursion & the call stack
packs.summary: Technical lesson (30 min of study time) · Print before vs after the recursive call · Tree recursion

cards.heading: Technical · 30 min
cards.body: A recursive function calls itself on a smaller input. It needs (1) a **base case** that stops, and (2) progress toward it. Each call gets its own frame on the **call stack**; too deep → **stack overflow**.

cards.heading: Visualise factorial(4)
cards.body: Study it line by line, then cover it and reproduce it from memory.
cards.codeSnippet:
fact(4) = 4 * fact(3)
            fact(3) = 3 * fact(2)
                        fact(2) = 2 * fact(1)
                                    fact(1) = 1      <- base case
                        = 2
            = 6
= 24

cards.heading: Print before vs after the recursive call
cards.body:
```
void f(int n){ if(n==0) return; print(n); f(n-1); }   // f(3) prints 3 2 1
void g(int n){ if(n==0) return; g(n-1); print(n); }   // g(3) prints 1 2 3
```

Code **after** the call runs while the stack **unwinds** — in reverse order.

cards.heading: Tree recursion
cards.body: `fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)` makes 2 calls each time → about 2ⁿ calls (exponential). fib(5) makes 15 calls. Fix with **memoisation** (store results) → O(n). That's the bridge to Dynamic Programming.

cards.heading: Common recursive questions
cards.body: Sum of digits, power(x,n) (fast power: x^n = (x^(n/2))² ), GCD (Euclid: gcd(a,b)=gcd(b,a%b)), reverse string, binary search, tree traversals, Tower of Hanoi (2ⁿ−1 moves).

cards.body:

packs.title: Time & space complexity (Big-O)
packs.summary: Technical lesson (30 min of study time) · How to compute

cards.heading: Technical · 30 min
cards.body: Big-O describes how running time **grows** as input n grows, ignoring constants. Ask: "If n doubles, what happens to the work?"

cards.heading: Overview
cards.body:
- **O(1)** — Name: constant · Example: array index, hash lookup (avg) · n=10⁶ ops ≈: 1
- **O(log n)** — Name: logarithmic · Example: binary search · n=10⁶ ops ≈: 20
- **O(n)** — Name: linear · Example: one loop · n=10⁶ ops ≈: 10⁶
- **O(n log n)** — Name: linearithmic · Example: merge sort, heap sort · n=10⁶ ops ≈: 2×10⁷
- **O(n²)** — Name: quadratic · Example: nested loops, bubble sort · n=10⁶ ops ≈: 10¹² ✗ too slow
- **O(2ⁿ)** — Name: exponential · Example: naive fib, all subsets · n=10⁶ ops ≈: impossible

cards.heading: Rule of thumb
cards.body: About 10⁸ simple operations per second. So n ≤ 10⁵ needs O(n log n) or better; n ≤ 10⁴ allows O(n²); n ≤ 20 allows O(2ⁿ).

packs.title: Arrays & strings: two pointers, sliding window, prefix sums
packs.summary: Technical lesson (40 min of study time) · Array basics · Pattern 1 — Two pointers · Pattern 2 — Sliding window

cards.heading: Technical · 40 min
cards.body: 40 minutes on **Arrays & strings: two pointers, sliding window, prefix sums**. You will cover: Array basics; Pattern 1 — Two pointers; Pattern 2 — Sliding window; Pattern 3 — Prefix sums; Kadane's algorithm (max subarray sum); Strings.

cards.heading: Array basics
cards.body: Contiguous memory, O(1) access by index, O(n) insert/delete in the middle. Index from 0 to n−1 — accessing n is out of bounds.

cards.heading: Pattern 1 — Two pointers
Pattern 2 — Sliding window
Pattern 3 — Prefix sums
cards.body: `pre[i] = a[0]+…+a[i-1]`. Sum of a[l..r] = `pre[r+1] − pre[l]` in O(1). Used for range-sum queries and "subarray sum equals k" (with a hash map).

cards.heading: Kadane's algorithm (max subarray sum)
cards.body: Study it line by line, then cover it and reproduce it from memory.
cards.codeSnippet:
int cur = 0, best = INT_MIN;
for (int x : a) { cur = max(x, cur + x); best = max(best, cur); }

cards.heading: Strings
cards.body: C: char array ending with `'\0'`. C++: `std::string`. Java: `String` is **immutable** — use `StringBuilder` for repeated appends (otherwise O(n²)). Common: reverse, palindrome, anagram (count frequencies), vowels count, character frequency, first non-repeating character, string compression ("aaabb" → "a3b2").

cards.heading: Technical · 40 min

cards.heading: Binary search (sorted data, O(log n))
cards.body: Study it line by line, then cover it and reproduce it from memory.

cards.heading: Analogy
cards.body: Guessing a number 1–100 with "higher/lower" — at most 7 guesses because 2⁷ = 128.

cards.heading: Sorting algorithms table (memorise)
cards.body:
- **Bubble** — Best: O(n)∗ · Average: O(n²) · Worst: O(n²) · Space: O(1) · Stable?: Yes · Idea: Swap adjacent; largest bubbles to end
- **Selection** — Best: O(n²) · Average: O(n²) · Worst: O(n²) · Space: O(1) · Stable?: No · Idea: Pick min, place at front
- **Insertion** — Best: O(n) · Average: O(n²) · Worst: O(n²) · Space: O(1) · Stable?: Yes · Idea: Insert each into sorted left part (like cards)
- **Merge** — Best: O(n log n) · Average: O(n log n) · Worst: O(n log n) · Space: O(n) · Stable?: Yes · Idea: Divide, sort halves, merge
- **Quick** — Best: O(n log n) · Average: O(n log n) · Worst: O(n²) · Space: O(log n) · Stable?: No · Idea: Pivot partition
- **Heap** — Best: O(n log n) · Average: O(n log n) · Worst: O(n log n) · Space: O(1) · Stable?: No · Idea: Build max-heap, extract
- **Counting** — Best: O(n + k) (k = value range) · Average: O(k) · Worst: Yes · Space: Count occurrences

∗Bubble is O(n) best only with the "no swaps → stop" optimisation. **Stable** = equal elements keep original order. Quick sort's worst case happens on already-sorted input with a bad pivot (first/last element).

cards.heading: Questions they ask
cards.body: "Number of swaps/passes in bubble sort for [5,1,4,2,8]", "array after 2nd pass of selection sort", "which sort is best for nearly sorted data?" → **insertion sort**. "Guaranteed O(n log n) + stable?" → **merge sort**.

packs.title: Trees & binary search trees
packs.summary: Technical lesson (40 min of study time) · Terms · Traversals (example tree: 1 at root, left 2 (children 4,5), right 3) · BST

cards.heading: Technical · 40 min
cards.body: A tree is a hierarchy: root at top, each node has children, nodes with no children are **leaves**. A **binary tree** has ≤ 2 children per node.

cards.heading: Terms
cards.body: **Height** = edges on the longest root-to-leaf path. **Depth** of a node = edges from root. Max nodes at level L = 2ᴸ. Max nodes in a binary tree of height h = 2^(h+1) − 1. A tree with n nodes has n−1 edges.

cards.heading: Traversals (example tree: 1 at root, left 2 (children 4,5), right 3)
BST
cards.body:
Left subtree < node < right subtree. **Inorder traversal of a BST gives sorted order** (favourite MCQ). Search/insert/delete: O(h) — O(log n) if balanced, O(n) if skewed (e.g., inserting sorted data). Balanced variants: AVL, Red-Black.

**Heap**: complete binary tree; max-heap parent ≥ children. Stored in an array: children of i are 2i+1 and 2i+2, parent (i−1)/2.

cards.heading: Common questions
cards.body: Height, count leaves, mirror a tree, check if BST (pass min/max bounds), lowest common ancestor, level order, diameter.

packs.title: Graphs: BFS, DFS & shortest paths
packs.summary: Technical lesson (40 min of study time) · Representation · BFS vs DFS · Shortest path algorithms

cards.heading: Technical · 40 min
cards.body: A graph = **vertices** (nodes) + **edges**. Directed/undirected, weighted/unweighted. Examples: roads between cities, friends network, course prerequisites.

cards.heading: Representation
cards.body: **Adjacency matrix**: V×V table, O(V²) space, O(1) edge check. **Adjacency list**: each node lists neighbours, O(V+E) space — preferred for sparse graphs.

cards.heading: BFS vs DFS
Shortest path algorithms
cards.body:
**Dijkstra**: non-negative weights, priority queue, O((V+E) log V). **Bellman-Ford**: handles negative weights, O(VE), detects negative cycles. **Floyd-Warshall**: all pairs, O(V³).

**Topological sort**: order tasks with dependencies (DAG only) — Kahn's algorithm (BFS with in-degrees). **MST**: Kruskal (sort edges + union-find), Prim (priority queue).

Grid problems ("number of islands", "rotting oranges") are graphs: each cell is a node with 4 neighbours.

packs.title: Dynamic programming: 1D and 2D
packs.summary: Technical lesson (45 min of study time) · 4-step recipe · 1D: Climbing stairs (1 or 2 steps) · 2D: Grid paths (move right/down)

cards.heading: Technical · 45 min
cards.body: DP = **recursion + remembering answers**. Use it when a problem has (1) **overlapping subproblems** and (2) **optimal substructure** (best answer built from best sub-answers).

cards.heading: Analogy
cards.body: Someone asks 1+1+1+1+1 = ? You count: 5. They add "+1". You say 6 instantly — you remembered the 5. That's DP.

cards.heading: 4-step recipe
cards.body:
1. **State**: what does dp[i] (or dp[i][j]) mean in words?
2. **Transition**: how dp[i] comes from smaller states.
3. **Base cases**.
4. **Order + answer**: fill so dependencies are ready; which cell is the answer?

cards.heading: 1D: Climbing stairs (1 or 2 steps)
cards.body:
```
dp[0] = 1; dp[1] = 1;                  // ways to reach step i
for (i = 2; i <= n; i++) dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2];
```

Others: house robber (`dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + a[i])`), coin change, longest increasing subsequence (`dp[i] = 1 + max(dp[j])` for j<i with a[j]<a[i]).

cards.heading: 2D: Grid paths (move right/down)
cards.body: Study it line by line, then cover it and reproduce it from memory.

cards.heading: 2D: Longest Common Subsequence (very likely in debugging round)
cards.body: Study it line by line, then cover it and reproduce it from memory.

cards.heading: 0/1 Knapsack
cards.body:
`dp[i][w] = max(dp[i-1][w], val[i] + dp[i-1][w - wt[i]])` if wt[i] ≤ w. Edit distance, matrix chain, min path sum are similar 2D tables.

**Memoisation** (top-down recursion + cache) vs **Tabulation** (bottom-up loops) — same complexity; tabulation avoids recursion depth limits.

cards.heading: Typical DP bugs
cards.body: Table size n instead of n+1 · wrong base row/column · using A[i] instead of A[i-1] when table is 1-indexed · loops in wrong order · not initialising (garbage values in C++ local arrays) · returning dp[m-1][n-1] instead of dp[m][n].

packs.title: OOP: the four pillars and Java/C++ details
packs.summary: Technical lesson (40 min of study time) · Polymorphism types · Abstract class vs interface (Java) · Other must-knows

cards.heading: Technical · 40 min
cards.body: OOP models software as **objects** (data + behaviour). A **class** is a blueprint (house plan); an **object** is an instance (an actual house).

cards.heading: Overview
cards.body:
- **Encapsulation** — Meaning: Bundle data + methods; hide internals (private fields, public getters/setters) · Example: BankAccount.balance is private; only deposit()/withdraw() change it with validation
- **Abstraction** — Meaning: Show *what*, hide *how* · Example: You call `car.start()`; you don't see the ignition logic. Abstract classes/interfaces
- **Inheritance** — Meaning: Child class reuses/extends parent ("is-a") · Example: Dog extends Animal
- **Polymorphism** — Meaning: Same call, different behaviour · Example: `shape.area()` works for Circle and Square

cards.heading: Polymorphism types
Abstract class vs interface (Java)
cards.body:
- **Methods** — Abstract class: Abstract + concrete · Interface: Abstract; default/static allowed since Java 8
- **Variables** — Abstract class: Any · Interface: public static final constants only
- **Inheritance** — Abstract class: extends one class · Interface: implements many (multiple inheritance of type)
- **Constructor** — Abstract class: Yes · Interface: No

cards.heading: Other must-knows
cards.body:
- **Constructor**: same name as class, no return type, runs at creation. Types: default, parameterised, copy (C++). **Destructor** in C++ (`~ClassName`); Java uses garbage collection.
- Java has **no multiple inheritance of classes** (diamond problem) — uses interfaces. C++ allows it (virtual inheritance solves the diamond).
- **Access modifiers**: private < default (package) < protected < public.
- **static**: belongs to the class, shared by all objects. **final** (Java): variable constant, method can't be overridden, class can't be extended.
- **this** = current object; **super** = parent.
- **Association / Aggregation (has-a, independent lifetime) / Composition (has-a, owned lifetime)**. Car has Engine (composition); Department has Professors (aggregation).
- **SOLID**: Single responsibility, Open/closed, Liskov substitution, Interface segregation, Dependency inversion.

packs.title: DBMS: keys, normalisation, ACID, indexing
packs.summary: Technical lesson (40 min of study time) · Keys · Normalisation — remove redundancy · Transactions: ACID

cards.heading: Technical · 40 min
cards.body: A **DBMS** stores and manages data; a **relational** DBMS (MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle) stores tables of rows and columns linked by keys. NoSQL (MongoDB, Redis, Cassandra) uses documents, key-value, wide-column or graph models — flexible schema, easy horizontal scaling.

cards.heading: Keys
cards.body:
- **Super key** — Any set of columns that uniquely identifies a row
- **Candidate key** — Minimal super key (no extra columns)
- **Primary key** — Chosen candidate key; unique + NOT NULL; one per table
- **Alternate key** — Candidate keys not chosen
- **Foreign key** — Column referring to another table's primary key → referential integrity
- **Composite key** — Primary key made of 2+ columns
- **Unique key** — Unique but allows NULL (one NULL in many DBs)

cards.heading: Normalisation — remove redundancy
cards.body:
- **1NF**: atomic values, no repeating groups ("phones: 98, 97" in one cell ✗).
- **2NF**: 1NF + no **partial dependency** (non-key column depends on only part of a composite key).
- **3NF**: 2NF + no **transitive dependency** (non-key → non-key, e.g., emp → dept_id → dept_name; move dept_name out).
- **BCNF**: every determinant is a candidate key.

Why normalise: avoid **insertion, update and deletion anomalies**. Denormalise deliberately for read speed.

cards.heading: Transactions: ACID
cards.body:
- **Atomicity** — All or nothing (bank transfer: debit and credit both happen or neither)
- **Consistency** — Valid state → valid state (constraints hold)
- **Isolation** — Concurrent transactions don't interfere
- **Durability** — Once committed, survives crashes

Commands: COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT. Problems without isolation: dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom read.

cards.heading: Indexing
cards.body:
An index (usually a **B+ tree**) is like a book's index — finds rows without scanning the whole table. Speeds up SELECT/WHERE/JOIN; slows INSERT/UPDATE and uses space. **Clustered** index = table physically ordered by it (one per table); **non-clustered** = separate structure pointing to rows.

**SQL command types**: DDL (CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE), DML (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE), DQL (SELECT), DCL (GRANT, REVOKE), TCL (COMMIT, ROLLBACK). DELETE (row-wise, can rollback, WHERE allowed) vs TRUNCATE (all rows, faster, resets) vs DROP (removes table).

packs.title: SQL queries you must write fluently
packs.summary: Technical lesson (45 min of study time) · Order of execution (explains many errors) · Joins · Top interview queries

cards.heading: Technical · 45 min
cards.body: Sample tables: `Employee(id, name, salary, dept_id, manager_id)`, `Department(id, dname)`.

cards.heading: Order of execution (explains many errors)
cards.body:
FROM → JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT. So you can't use a SELECT alias in WHERE, and you filter groups with **HAVING**, rows with **WHERE**.

```
-- average salary per department, only departments with avg > 50000
SELECT d.dname, AVG(e.salary) AS avg_sal
FROM Employee e JOIN Department d ON e.dept_id = d.id
GROUP BY d.dname
HAVING AVG(e.salary) > 50000
ORDER BY avg_sal DESC;
```

cards.heading: Joins
cards.body:
- **INNER** — Only matching rows in both
- **LEFT** — All left rows + matches (NULL if none)
- **RIGHT** — All right rows + matches
- **FULL OUTER** — All rows from both
- **CROSS** — Every combination (m × n rows)
- **SELF** — Table joined to itself (employee–manager)

cards.heading: Top interview queries
Traps
cards.body: `= NULL` never works — use `IS NULL`. `COUNT(*)` counts all rows; `COUNT(col)` skips NULLs. `UNION` removes duplicates, `UNION ALL` keeps them (faster). RANK gives gaps (1,1,3); DENSE_RANK doesn't (1,1,2); ROW_NUMBER is always unique.

packs.title: Operating systems essentials
packs.summary: Technical lesson (40 min of study time) · Process vs thread · CPU scheduling · Deadlock

cards.heading: Technical · 40 min
cards.body: 40 minutes on **Operating systems essentials**. You will cover: Process vs thread; CPU scheduling; Deadlock; Synchronisation; Memory.

cards.heading: Process vs thread
cards.body:
- **What** — Process: Program in execution · Thread: Lightweight unit inside a process
- **Memory** — Process: Own address space · Thread: Shares process memory (heap, code), own stack
- **Switch cost** — Process: High · Thread: Low
- **Analogy** — Process: A restaurant · Thread: Cooks inside sharing one kitchen

**Process states**: New → Ready → Running → Waiting (I/O) → Terminated. A **context switch** saves one process's state (PCB) and loads another's.

cards.heading: CPU scheduling
cards.body:
- **FCFS** — Idea: First come first served · Note: Convoy effect (short jobs wait behind long)
- **SJF / SRTF** — Idea: Shortest job first (preemptive = SRTF) · Note: Minimum avg waiting time; starvation possible
- **Round Robin** — Idea: Each gets a time quantum · Note: Fair, good response time; time-sharing
- **Priority** — Idea: Highest priority first · Note: Starvation → fix by aging

Turnaround time = completion − arrival. Waiting time = turnaround − burst.

cards.heading: Deadlock
cards.body: Two+ processes each wait for a resource the other holds (two cars on a one-lane bridge). **Four necessary conditions (Coffman)**: Mutual exclusion, Hold and wait, No preemption, Circular wait. Break any one to prevent it. **Banker's algorithm** avoids deadlock by checking safe states.

cards.heading: Synchronisation
cards.body: **Race condition**: result depends on timing of threads (two threads doing count++). **Critical section** protected by **mutex** (lock, one owner) or **semaphore** (counter; binary or counting). Classic problems: producer–consumer, readers–writers, dining philosophers.

cards.heading: Memory
cards.body:
**Paging**: memory split into fixed-size pages/frames → no external fragmentation. **Segmentation**: variable-size logical segments. **Virtual memory**: use disk to give the illusion of more RAM; **page fault** when a page isn't in RAM. Replacement: FIFO, LRU, Optimal. **Thrashing**: too many page faults, system spends time swapping. **Belady's anomaly**: more frames → more faults in FIFO.

Also: **kernel** (core of OS), user vs kernel mode, system calls, **fragmentation** (internal vs external), **cache**, stack vs heap memory.

packs.title: Computer networks essentials
packs.summary: Technical lesson (40 min of study time) · OSI 7 layers (top → bottom): "All People Seem To Need Data Processing" · TCP vs UDP · What happens when you type a URL

cards.heading: Technical · 40 min
cards.body: 40 minutes on **Computer networks essentials**. You will cover: OSI 7 layers (top → bottom): "All People Seem To Need Data Processing"; TCP vs UDP; What happens when you type a URL; Must-know facts.

cards.heading: OSI 7 layers (top → bottom): "All People Seem To Need Data Processing"
cards.body:
- **7** — Layer: Application · Job: User-facing protocols · Examples: HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, SMTP, DNS
- **6** — Layer: Presentation · Job: Format, encryption, compression · Examples: SSL/TLS, JPEG
- **5** — Layer: Session · Job: Manage sessions · Examples: RPC
- **4** — Layer: Transport · Job: End-to-end delivery, ports · Examples: TCP, UDP
- **3** — Layer: Network · Job: Routing, IP addresses · Examples: IP, ICMP, routers
- **2** — Layer: Data link · Job: Frames, MAC addresses · Examples: Ethernet, switches
- **1** — Layer: Physical · Job: Bits over wire/air · Examples: Cables, hubs

TCP/IP model has 4 layers: Application, Transport, Internet, Network Access.

cards.heading: TCP vs UDP
cards.body:
- **Connection-oriented (3-way handshake: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK)** — Connectionless
- **Reliable, ordered, retransmits lost packets** — No guarantee, faster, lower overhead
- **Web, email, file transfer** — Video calls, gaming, DNS, streaming

cards.heading: What happens when you type a URL
cards.body:
1. DNS resolves domain → IP (browser cache → OS → resolver → root → TLD → authoritative).
2. TCP handshake with the server (port 443).
3. TLS handshake (certificate check, key exchange) → encrypted channel.
4. HTTP request (GET /) → server processes → response (HTML, status 200).
5. Browser parses, fetches CSS/JS/images, renders.

cards.heading: Must-know facts
cards.body: Ports: HTTP 80, HTTPS 443, SSH 22, FTP 21, SMTP 25, DNS 53, MySQL 3306, PostgreSQL 5432. IPv4 = 32 bits (192.168.1.1), IPv6 = 128 bits. Private ranges: 10.x, 172.16–31.x, 192.168.x. **Subnet mask** /24 = 255.255.255.0 → 256 addresses (254 usable hosts). **NAT** maps private IPs to one public IP. **DHCP** assigns IPs automatically. **ARP** maps IP → MAC. Devices: hub (L1, broadcasts), switch (L2, MAC), router (L3, IP). **Firewall** filters traffic; **VPN** encrypts a tunnel; **CDN** serves content from servers near users; **load balancer** spreads requests.

packs.title: Web & APIs: client–server, REST, HTTP, auth
packs.summary: Technical lesson (45 min of study time) · Client–server · REST APIs · Status codes

cards.heading: Technical · 45 min
cards.body: 45 minutes on **Web & APIs: client–server, REST, HTTP, auth**. You will cover: Client–server; REST APIs; Status codes; API key vs token (asked explicitly in 2027 syllabus).

cards.heading: Client–server
cards.body: The **client** (browser, mobile app) sends requests; the **server** processes and responds. Like a restaurant: you (client) order, the kitchen (server) cooks, the waiter (API) carries messages.

cards.heading: REST APIs
cards.body:
**REST** = an architectural style using HTTP. Resources are URLs (`/users/42`); actions are HTTP methods; data usually in **JSON**. Principles: client–server, **stateless** (each request carries everything needed; server keeps no session between requests), cacheable, uniform interface, layered system.

- **GET** — Action: Read · Example: GET /orders/7 · Idempotent?: Yes · Safe?: Yes
- **POST** — Action: Create · Example: POST /orders · Idempotent?: No · Safe?: No
- **PUT** — Action: Replace whole resource · Example: PUT /orders/7 · Idempotent?: Yes · Safe?: No
- **PATCH** — Action: Partial update · Example: PATCH /orders/7 {status} · Idempotent?: Not guaranteed · Safe?: No
- **DELETE** — Action: Remove · Example: DELETE /orders/7 · Idempotent?: Yes · Safe?: No

**Idempotent** = calling it many times has the same effect as once (pressing a lift button repeatedly). That's why payment APIs use **idempotency keys** on POST.

cards.heading: Status codes
cards.body:
- **2xx success** — 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content
- **3xx redirect** — 301 Moved Permanently, 302 Found, 304 Not Modified
- **4xx client error** — 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized (not logged in / bad credentials), 403 Forbidden (logged in but no permission), 404 Not Found, 405 Method Not Allowed, 409 Conflict, 422 Unprocessable, 429 Too Many Requests
- **5xx server error** — 500 Internal Server Error, 502 Bad Gateway, 503 Service Unavailable, 504 Gateway Timeout

cards.heading: API key vs token (asked explicitly in 2027 syllabus)
cards.body:
- **Identifies** — API key: The application/project calling the API · Access token (e.g., JWT / OAuth): The user + their permissions
- **Lifetime** — API key: Long-lived, until revoked · Access token (e.g., JWT / OAuth): Short-lived (minutes/hours), refreshed via refresh token
- **Typical use** — API key: Server-to-server, usage tracking, rate limiting · Access token (e.g., JWT / OAuth): User login sessions, delegated access ("Sign in with Google")
- **Risk** — API key: If leaked, works until rotated — never put in frontend code or Git · Access token (e.g., JWT / OAuth): Limited damage due to expiry and scopes

**Authentication** = who are you (login). **Authorization** = what may you do (permissions). **JWT** = header.payload.signature, Base64URL-encoded, *signed not encrypted* (anyone can read the payload, nobody can change it without the key). **OAuth 2.0** = delegated authorization framework; **OpenID Connect** adds identity on top. Sessions use server-stored state + cookie; tokens are stateless.

Also: **CORS** (browser blocks cross-origin requests unless the server allows them), **GraphQL** (client asks for exact fields, one endpoint), **WebSockets** (two-way real-time), **webhooks** (server calls your URL when an event happens), **rate limiting**, **pagination**, API **versioning** (/v1/).

packs.title: Git & version control
packs.summary: Technical lesson (25 min of study time)

cards.heading: Technical · 25 min
cards.body: 25 minutes on **Git & version control**. Read it once for the idea, then once more to say it aloud.

cards.heading: The essentials
cards.body:
Git tracks changes so teams can work in parallel and undo mistakes. Three areas: **working directory** → (`git add`) → **staging area** → (`git commit`) → **local repository** → (`git push`) → **remote** (GitHub/GitLab).

- **git init / clone** — Create repo / copy remote repo
- **git status / log / diff** — See state / history / changes
- **git branch feature-x · git checkout -b feature-x (or git switch -c)** — Create / create+switch branch
- **git merge feature-x** — Combine branch into current; may create a merge commit
- **git rebase main** — Replay your commits on top of main → linear history (don't rebase shared/public branches)
- **git fetch** — Download remote changes, don't merge
- **git pull** — fetch + merge (or rebase)
- **git stash** — Temporarily shelve uncommitted changes
- **git revert <commit>** — New commit that undoes an old one (safe for shared history)
- **git reset --soft/--mixed/--hard** — Move branch pointer; --hard discards changes
- **git cherry-pick <commit>** — Apply one specific commit to current branch

**Merge conflict**: same lines changed in both branches. Git marks `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>`; you edit to the correct version, then add + commit. **.gitignore** lists files not to track (node_modules, .env). **Pull request** = request to merge with code review. Workflows: feature branching, GitFlow, trunk-based development.

packs.title: Cloud, Docker, DevOps & Agile
packs.summary: Technical lesson (45 min of study time) · Cloud service models (pizza analogy) · Containers & Docker · DevOps & CI/CD

cards.heading: Technical · 45 min
cards.body: 45 minutes on **Cloud, Docker, DevOps & Agile**. You will cover: Cloud service models (pizza analogy); Containers & Docker; DevOps & CI/CD; Agile & Scrum.

cards.heading: Cloud service models (pizza analogy)
cards.body:
- **On-premise** — You manage: Everything · Provider manages: Nothing · Example: Own data centre · Pizza: Make at home
- **IaaS** — You manage: OS, runtime, apps, data · Provider manages: Hardware, network, virtualisation · Example: AWS EC2, GCP Compute Engine, Azure VMs · Pizza: Take-and-bake
- **PaaS** — You manage: Apps, data · Provider manages: + OS, runtime · Example: Heroku, Google App Engine, Cloud Run, Azure App Service · Pizza: Delivery
- **SaaS** — You manage: Just use it · Provider manages: Everything · Example: Gmail, Salesforce, Office 365 · Pizza: Dine out

**Deployment models**: public, private, hybrid, multi-cloud. **Benefits**: pay-as-you-go, elasticity (auto-scale up/down), high availability across regions/zones. **Serverless** (AWS Lambda, Cloud Functions): run functions without managing servers, pay per execution. **Scaling**: vertical (bigger machine) vs horizontal (more machines). **Object storage**: S3/GCS.

cards.heading: Containers & Docker
cards.body:
A **container** packages an app with its dependencies so it runs the same everywhere ("works on my machine" solved). Containers share the host OS kernel → lightweight, start in seconds. A **VM** includes a full guest OS → heavier.

**Dockerfile** (recipe) → `docker build` → **image** (read-only template) → `docker run` → **container** (running instance). **Registry**: Docker Hub. **docker-compose**: multi-container apps. **Kubernetes**: orchestrates many containers — scheduling, auto-scaling, self-healing, rolling updates; units: **pod**, deployment, service, node, cluster.

cards.heading: DevOps & CI/CD
cards.body: DevOps = culture + practices joining development and operations for faster, reliable releases. **CI (Continuous Integration)**: every push is built and tested automatically. **CD**: Continuous **Delivery** (always ready to deploy, manual approval) vs Continuous **Deployment** (auto to production). Tools: GitHub Actions, Jenkins, GitLab CI. **Infrastructure as Code**: Terraform. Monitoring: Prometheus, Grafana. Deployment strategies: blue-green, canary, rolling.

cards.heading: Agile & Scrum
cards.body: **Agile**: iterative, small increments, customer feedback, responding to change (vs **Waterfall**: fixed sequential phases). **Scrum**: **sprints** (1–4 weeks); roles — **Product Owner** (owns backlog/priorities), **Scrum Master** (facilitates, removes blockers), **Development team**; ceremonies — sprint planning, **daily stand-up** (yesterday/today/blockers), sprint review (demo), **retrospective** (improve process); artifacts — product backlog, sprint backlog, increment. **User story**: "As a [user], I want [goal] so that [benefit]". Story points estimate effort. **Kanban**: visual board, limit work-in-progress, continuous flow.

packs.title: Cybersecurity fundamentals
packs.summary: Technical lesson (35 min of study time) · Common attacks · Hashing vs encryption vs encoding

cards.heading: Technical · 35 min
cards.body: **CIA triad**: **Confidentiality** (only authorised people read), **Integrity** (data not tampered), **Availability** (accessible when needed).

cards.heading: Common attacks
cards.body:
- **SQL injection** — What happens: Input like `' OR '1'='1` changes your SQL query · Defence: Parameterised queries / prepared statements, ORM, input validation
- **XSS (Cross-site scripting)** — What happens: Attacker's script runs in other users' browsers · Defence: Escape/encode output, Content Security Policy, sanitise input
- **CSRF** — What happens: Logged-in user tricked into sending an unwanted request · Defence: CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies
- **Phishing** — What happens: Fake emails/sites steal credentials · Defence: Awareness, MFA, verify sender/URL
- **DDoS** — What happens: Flood of traffic makes service unavailable · Defence: Rate limiting, CDN/WAF, auto-scaling
- **Man-in-the-middle** — What happens: Intercepts traffic · Defence: HTTPS/TLS, certificate validation
- **Brute force** — What happens: Guessing passwords · Defence: Account lockout, MFA, strong policy
- **Ransomware / malware** — What happens: Encrypts/steals data · Defence: Backups, patching, least privilege

cards.heading: Hashing vs encryption vs encoding
cards.body:
- **Encoding** — Reversible?: Yes, no key · Purpose: Data format · Example: Base64, URL encoding
- **Encryption** — Reversible?: Yes, with key · Purpose: Confidentiality · Example: AES (symmetric, one key), RSA (asymmetric, public/private)
- **Hashing** — Reversible?: No (one-way) · Purpose: Integrity, password storage · Example: SHA-256; passwords with bcrypt/argon2 + salt

**Principles**: least privilege, defence in depth, zero trust ("never trust, always verify"), MFA, patch management, secrets in a vault/env vars (never in code). **OWASP Top 10** = list of the most critical web app risks (broken access control, injection, cryptographic failures, etc.).
