packs.title: SDLC, testing & software engineering basics
packs.summary: Technical lesson (25 min of study time) · SDLC phases · Testing levels and types

cards.heading: Technical · 25 min
cards.body: 25 minutes on **SDLC, testing & software engineering basics**. You will cover: SDLC phases; Testing levels and types.

cards.heading: SDLC phases
cards.body:
Requirement analysis → Design → Implementation (coding) → Testing → Deployment → Maintenance.

- **Waterfall** — Fixed, clear requirements; sequential; changes costly
- **V-Model** — Each dev phase has a matching test phase
- **Iterative / Incremental** — Build in pieces
- **Spiral** — Risk-driven, large projects
- **Agile** — Changing requirements, frequent delivery

cards.heading: Testing levels and types
cards.body:
- **Unit** (single function, by developers, e.g., JUnit/Jest) → **Integration** (modules together) → **System** (whole app) → **Acceptance/UAT** (client validates).
- **Black-box** (test inputs/outputs, no code knowledge) vs **White-box** (test internal paths). Grey-box = partial.
- **Regression**: re-test after changes that old features still work. **Smoke**: quick check that the build basically works. **Sanity**: narrow check after a small fix. **Performance/Load/Stress**. **Alpha** (internal) vs **Beta** (real users).
- Techniques: **equivalence partitioning** (group inputs that behave the same), **boundary value analysis** (test at edges: for 1–100 test 0, 1, 100, 101).
- **TDD**: write a failing test → make it pass → refactor.

**Error vs defect/bug vs failure**: human mistake → bug in code → system fails at runtime. **Verification** ("are we building the product right?") vs **Validation** ("are we building the right product?").

Design principles: DRY (don't repeat yourself), KISS, YAGNI; **coupling** (dependency between modules — keep low) vs **cohesion** (focus within a module — keep high). Design patterns: Singleton, Factory, Observer, MVC.

packs.title: The debugging method & bug taxonomy
packs.summary: Debugging lesson (35 min of study time) · The 4-step loop: Review → Identify → Fix → Validate · Bug checklist — scan in this order

cards.heading: Debugging · 35 min
cards.body: The debugging round gives you **one broken program (~20 min)** in C, C++ or Java. You must fix it with **minimal changes** — not rewrite it. Reported topics include trees, graphs and 2D DP, but the bugs themselves are usually small.

cards.heading: The 4-step loop: Review → Identify → Fix → Validate
cards.body:
1. **Review (3–4 min)**: read the problem statement. Write 1–2 tiny test inputs with expected outputs by hand. Read the code top-down: what does each function intend?
2. **Identify (6–8 min)**: run it (if allowed) or trace your small input. Compare expected vs actual at each step. The first point where they differ is near the bug.
3. **Fix (2–3 min)**: change the smallest thing. Keep signatures and I/O format unchanged.
4. **Validate (3–4 min)**: run normal + edge inputs: empty, single element, all equal, negatives, maximum size, n = 0/1.

cards.heading: Bug checklist — scan in this order
cards.body:
- **Boundaries** — `<` vs `<=`, loop start 0 vs 1, `n` vs `n-1`, array size n vs n+1
- **Initialisation** — sum/count not set to 0; max initialised to 0 instead of INT_MIN or a[0]; dp table not initialised
- **Operators** — `=` vs `==`, `&` vs `&&`, `/` vs `%`, `+=` vs `=`, wrong comparison direction
- **Types** — integer division (1/2 = 0), overflow (use long), char vs int
- **Control flow** — missing `break` in switch, misplaced `return` inside loop, wrong else attachment, stray semicolon `for(...);`
- **Recursion** — missing/incorrect base case, not returning the recursive result, wrong argument (n instead of n-1)
- **Variables** — wrong variable used (i vs j), shadowing, updated in wrong place, swap done incorrectly
- **Graphs/trees** — visited not marked/reset, null child not checked, queue/stack misuse
- **Output** — wrong format, missing newline/space, printing inside loop

cards.heading: Use print debugging
cards.body: Add a temporary `print(i, sum)` inside the loop to see where values go wrong — then remove it. Syntax errors: read the compiler's first error line only; later errors are often caused by the first.

cards.heading: Three bug kinds
cards.body: **Syntax/compile-time** (missing semicolon, type mismatch) · **Runtime** (crash: divide by zero, null pointer, index out of bounds, stack overflow) · **Logical** (runs but wrong answer — the hardest and most common in this round).

cards.body:

packs.title: C / C++ specific bugs
packs.summary: Debugging lesson (35 min of study time)

cards.heading: Debugging · 35 min
cards.body: 35 minutes on **C / C++ specific bugs**. Read it once for the idea, then once more to say it aloud.

cards.heading: The essentials
cards.body:
- **Array out of bounds (no error, garbage!)** — Example: `int a[5]; for(i=0;i<=5;i++)` · Fix: `i<5`
- **Uninitialised local variable** — Example: `int sum; sum += x;` · Fix: `int sum = 0;`
- **Pass by value when change is needed** — Example: `void swap(int a,int b)` · Fix: `void swap(int &a,int &b)` (C++) or pointers `int *a` (C)
- **Dangling pointer** — Example: returning address of a local variable · Fix: allocate with new/malloc or return by value
- **Memory leak** — Example: `new` without `delete`, `malloc` without `free` · Fix: free memory; prefer vector / smart pointers
- **Null pointer dereference** — Example: `node->next->val` when next is NULL · Fix: check `if(node && node->next)`
- **String compare** — Example: `if (s1 == s2)` with char arrays compares addresses · Fix: `strcmp(s1,s2)==0`
- **Missing null terminator / buffer size** — Example: `char s[5] = "hello";` · Fix: `char s[6]`
- **sizeof on array parameter** — Example: `sizeof(arr)/sizeof(arr[0])` inside a function = pointer size · Fix: pass n separately
- **Integer overflow** — Example: `int prod = a*b;` with large values · Fix: `long long prod = 1LL*a*b;`
- **Integer division** — Example: `double avg = sum / n;` · Fix: `(double)sum / n`
- **Iterator invalidation** — Example: erasing from a vector inside a range-for · Fix: use `it = v.erase(it)`
- **scanf missing &** — Example: `scanf("%d", x);` · Fix: `scanf("%d", &x);`
- **Wrong format specifier** — Example: `printf("%d", 3.5)` · Fix: `%f` / `%lf` / `%lld` for long long

packs.title: Java specific bugs
packs.summary: Debugging lesson (30 min of study time)

cards.heading: Debugging · 30 min
cards.body: 30 minutes on **Java specific bugs**. Read it once for the idea, then once more to say it aloud.

cards.heading: The essentials
cards.body:
- **String compare with ==** — Example: `if (s == "yes")` compares references · Fix: `s.equals("yes")` or `"yes".equals(s)` (null-safe)
- **NullPointerException** — Example: calling a method on null · Fix: null check, Optional, initialise fields
- **ArrayIndexOutOfBounds** — Example: `arr[arr.length]` · Fix: last index is `length-1`
- **Integer caching trap** — Example: `Integer a=1000,b=1000; a==b` → false · Fix: `a.equals(b)`
- **Overflow** — Example: `int` sum of large values · Fix: `long`
- **Strings are immutable** — Example: `s.toUpperCase();` (result ignored) · Fix: `s = s.toUpperCase();`
- **String concatenation in loop** — Example: `s += c` 10⁵ times → O(n²) · Fix: `StringBuilder`
- **ConcurrentModificationException** — Example: removing from a list inside for-each · Fix: Iterator.remove() or removeIf()
- **Missing break in switch** — Example: fall-through executes next cases · Fix: add `break`
- **Static vs instance** — Example: calling instance method from `static main` · Fix: create object or make method static
- **equals without hashCode** — Example: objects in HashSet not found · Fix: override both consistently
- **Array length syntax** — Example: `arr.length()` / `str.length` · Fix: array: `.length`; String: `.length()`; List: `.size()`
- **char arithmetic** — Example: `char c = 'a' + i;` (compile error with variable) · Fix: `(char)('a' + i)`
- **Scanner nextInt then nextLine** — Example: nextLine returns empty · Fix: consume the leftover newline

packs.title: JavaScript, React & Node bugs (Super Dream / Alpha track)
packs.summary: Debugging lesson (45 min of study time) · JavaScript core · React · Node / Express

cards.heading: Debugging · 45 min
cards.body: Candidate reports for the higher-package track mention debugging **React frontend projects with an AI co-pilot**. You build React/Node apps already — this lesson lists the bugs graders love.

cards.heading: JavaScript core
cards.body:
- **Loose equality** — Example: `0 == ''` → true, `'5' == 5` → true · Fix: use `===`
- **var in loop closures** — Example: `for(var i=0;i<3;i++) setTimeout(()=>log(i))` → 3,3,3 · Fix: `let i` → 0,1,2
- **Missing await** — Example: `const data = fetch(url).json()` · Fix: `const res = await fetch(url); const data = await res.json();`
- **forEach with async** — Example: `arr.forEach(async x => await save(x))` doesn't wait · Fix: `for...of` with await or `Promise.all(arr.map(save))`
- **this lost** — Example: passing `obj.method` as callback · Fix: arrow function or `.bind(obj)`
- **Mutating while iterating / sort mutates** — Example: `arr.sort()` sorts numbers as strings: [10,9,1] → [1,10,9] · Fix: `arr.sort((a,b)=>a-b)`
- **Floating point** — Example: `0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3` → false · Fix: compare with tolerance / integer paise
- **typeof null** — Example: returns "object" · Fix: check `x === null`
- **Optional access** — Example: `user.address.city` crashes if address undefined · Fix: `user?.address?.city`

cards.heading: React
Node / Express
cards.body:
- Unhandled promise rejections — wrap awaits in try/catch or use an error middleware.
- Blocking the event loop with heavy sync work (big loops, `fs.readFileSync` in a request handler).
- Forgetting `return` after `res.send()` → "Cannot set headers after they are sent".
- Missing `express.json()` middleware → `req.body` undefined.
- Wrong middleware order (auth placed after the route).
- SQL/NoSQL injection from unvalidated `req.query`.
- Not awaiting DB calls → returning a Promise in the response.

packs.title: AI-assisted coding round: the 5-step workflow
packs.summary: AI-assisted coding lesson (40 min of study time)

cards.heading: AI-assisted coding · 40 min
cards.body: 40 minutes on **AI-assisted coding round: the 5-step workflow**. Read it once for the idea, then once more to say it aloud.

cards.heading: The essentials
cards.body:
~45 min. You solve a coding task by **directing an AI assistant**. You are graded on the **process**: how you understand, prompt, review and validate — not only the final code. Reported scoring areas: **AI literacy, prompt quality, problem-solving approach, review & adapt**.

- **1. Understand** — What you do: Restate the problem in your words; note inputs, outputs, constraints, edge cases; pick an approach and complexity target · Time: 5–7 min
- **2. Plan / Prompt** — What you do: Structured prompt (role, context, task, constraints, format). Ask for approach first if unsure · Time: 5 min
- **3. Generate** — What you do: Let AI produce code for one piece at a time · Time: 5 min
- **4. Review & Adapt** — What you do: Read every line; trace an example; fix or re-prompt with *specific* feedback · Time: 10–15 min
- **5. Validate** — What you do: Run tests: normal, edge, large; check complexity; final clean-up · Time: 8–10 min

cards.heading: Worked mini-example: "Return the first non-repeating character in a string, or '_' if none"
cards.body:
**Understand**: input lowercase string up to 10⁵; output char. Edge: empty, all repeating, single char. Approach: count frequencies (26-array), second pass finds first count==1 → O(n).

**Prompt**: "You are a Java expert. Write `char firstUnique(String s)`. Use an int[26] frequency array and two passes, O(n) time, O(1) space. Return '_' if none or s is empty. Include 5 JUnit-style test cases (empty, 'a', 'aabb', 'leetcode' → 'l', 'aabbc' → 'c'). Return only code."

**Review**: AI used `HashMap` instead → acceptable but violates stated constraint → re-prompt: "Replace HashMap with int[26] as specified; keep everything else."

**Validate**: run tests; check 'z' indexing (`c - 'a'`).

cards.heading: What loses marks
cards.body: Pasting the whole question with "solve" · accepting first output · many vague re-prompts ("still wrong, fix") · not testing · not understanding the code you submit (they may ask you to explain).

packs.title: AI-assisted feature development (React/Node example)
packs.summary: AI-assisted coding lesson (40 min of study time) · Example feature: "Add search with debounce + pagination to the Products page"

cards.heading: AI-assisted coding · 40 min
cards.body: The higher track reportedly asks you to **build a feature in an existing project** with AI. The professional pattern: **spec → small tasks → prompt each → integrate → test**.

cards.heading: Example feature: "Add search with debounce + pagination to the Products page"
cards.body:
**1. Read the existing code first**: where is the products list? What API does it call? Which state library? Naming style?

**2. Write a mini-spec** (this is also your best prompt context):

```
Feature: product search
- Input box above product list; filters by name (case-insensitive)
- Debounce 300 ms; call GET /api/products?q=<term>&page=<n>&limit=10
- Show "No products found" when empty; show spinner while loading
- Pagination: Prev/Next; reset to page 1 when the search term changes
- Backend (Express + MongoDB): add q, page, limit query params; validate limit <= 50;
  use regex with escaped user input (avoid ReDoS/injection); return {items, total, page}
Acceptance tests: typing "lap" shows laptops; rapid typing makes one request; page 2 works
```

**3. Prompt chain (one concern per prompt)**

1. "Here is `productRoutes.js` [paste]. Add q/page/limit support as per spec [paste]. Keep the existing response shape plus `total`. Return only the modified route."
2. "Here is `ProductList.jsx` [paste]. Add a search input with a 300 ms debounce using a custom `useDebounce` hook, and Prev/Next pagination. Use the existing `api.get` helper. Don't add new libraries."
3. "Write Jest + React Testing Library tests for: debounce fires once, page resets on new term, empty state."

**4. Review**: cleanup of the debounce timer in useEffect? page reset bug? escaped regex? limit validated? loading state on error?

**5. Validate**: run app, test the acceptance criteria manually, run tests.

cards.heading: Why this impresses
cards.body: It shows you treat AI like a fast junior teammate: you give clear requirements, review its pull request, and own the result.

packs.title: Reviewing AI output: the checklist
packs.summary: AI-assisted coding lesson (30 min of study time) · Choosing good test cases

cards.heading: AI-assisted coding · 30 min
cards.body: 30 minutes on **Reviewing AI output: the checklist**. You will cover: Choosing good test cases.

cards.heading: Overview
cards.body:
- **Spec match** — Same signature? Uses only allowed libraries? Output format exact?
- **Correctness** — Trace one normal example by hand. Does the loop cover all elements?
- **Edge cases** — Empty, single, duplicates, negatives, zero, max size, null, unicode
- **Complexity** — Hidden O(n²) (e.g., `list.contains` inside a loop, string += in loop)?
- **Hallucinations** — Do all functions/APIs actually exist in this language version?
- **Security** — SQL concatenation, unescaped HTML, secrets in code, no input validation
- **Resources** — Files/connections closed, timers cleared, memory freed
- **Readability** — Clear names, no dead code, comments where needed

cards.heading: Choosing good test cases
cards.body: A good test set includes: a typical case, smallest input, empty input, boundary values (first/last element, exact limit), duplicates, negative numbers, a case where the answer is "none", and a large input for performance. **Boundary value analysis**: if valid range is 1..100, test 0, 1, 2, 99, 100, 101.

cards.heading: Re-prompting well
cards.body:
✗ "It's wrong, fix it."

packs.title: Grid Challenge: working memory under distraction
packs.summary: Cognitive lesson (15 min of study time) · Technique

cards.heading: Cognitive · 15 min
cards.body: **Format**: a dot lights up in a grid (often 4×4). Then you answer a distraction question (e.g., "is this pattern symmetrical?"). Then another dot, another distraction… At the end, click all dot positions **in order**. Difficulty increases as you succeed.

cards.heading: Technique
cards.body:
- **Encode as a path/shape**, not separate dots: "top-left → middle → bottom-right = a diagonal slash".
- Give positions short names: rows A–D, columns 1–4 → "A1, C3, B4". Rehearse silently while answering the symmetry question.
- Symmetry questions: check the vertical mirror line — compare column 1 with 4 and 2 with 3, row by row. Answer fast, don't over-check.
- Accuracy beats speed. If unsure of the order, place the ones you're sure of first.

The Grid Challenge game itself is not in this app — practise it on the original prep page (levels grow from 3 to 7 dots).

packs.title: Motion Challenge: planning in fewest moves
packs.summary: Cognitive lesson (15 min of study time) · Technique

cards.heading: Cognitive · 15 min
cards.body: **Format**: get the **red ball into the hole** by moving the ball and blocks around a grid with walls. Scored on solving in the **minimum number of moves**, within time.

cards.heading: Technique
cards.body:
1. **Work backwards**: which cell must the ball come from to enter the hole? What blocks that path?
2. Identify the **blocking pieces** and where they can go (empty cells not on the ball's route).
3. **Plan the full sequence before touching anything**. Count moves in your head.
4. Avoid "exploring" moves — every extra move costs score.

packs.title: Inductive & deductive logic (pattern and matrix puzzles)
packs.summary: Cognitive lesson (25 min of study time) · Inductive (find the rule) · Deductive (Latin square / symbol matrix)

cards.heading: Cognitive · 25 min
cards.body: 25 minutes on **Inductive & deductive logic (pattern and matrix puzzles)**. You will cover: Inductive (find the rule); Deductive (Latin square / symbol matrix).

cards.heading: Inductive (find the rule)
cards.body:
Series of figures/numbers → choose the next one. Check one property at a time: **count** (sides, dots, lines), **position/rotation** (45°, 90° steps, clockwise), **shading** (alternating), **size**, **add/subtract** elements. The correct rule explains **every** step.

Number series patterns: +k, ×k, squares (1,4,9,16), cubes, primes, alternating two series (2, 10, 4, 20, 6, 30…), differences of differences (1, 2, 4, 7, 11 → differences 1,2,3,4), Fibonacci-like, n² ± 1, ×2+1.

cards.heading: Deductive (Latin square / symbol matrix)
cards.body:
An N×N grid where each symbol appears **exactly once per row and column** (like mini Sudoku). Find the symbol for the "?" cell.

1. Look at the ? cell's row: which symbols are present?
2. Look at its column: which are present?
3. The answer = the symbol missing from **both**. If still ambiguous, fill another cell first (one with the fewest options).

cards.heading: Example (4×4: ★ ● ▲ ■)
cards.body: Row of ? has ★, ▲. Column of ? has ●. Missing from row: ●, ■. Exclude column's ● → answer **■**.

cards.heading: Switch Challenge
cards.body: Four symbols go into a "switch" and come out rearranged. Choose the code (e.g., 3-1-4-2) that produces the output. Method: number the input positions 1–4. For each output position, write which input position that symbol came from. Output = (symbol from position 3, then 1, then 4, then 2) → code **3142**.

cards.heading: Example
cards.body: Input: ▲ ● ■ ★ (positions 1 2 3 4). Output: ■ ▲ ★ ●. ■ was at 3, ▲ at 1, ★ at 4, ● at 2 → **3142**.

cards.heading: Digit Challenge
cards.body: Fill blanks with digits (often 1–9, no repeats) to make an equation true: `_ × _ − _ = 23`. Start with the operator that constrains most (× and ÷), try values near the target (5×5 = 25, 25 − 2 = 23 ✓ but digits must differ → 4×6 = 24, 24 − 1 = 23 ✓).

packs.title: Logical reasoning: series, coding-decoding, relations, syllogisms
packs.summary: Cognitive lesson (40 min of study time) · Coding–decoding · Blood relations · Direction sense

cards.heading: Cognitive · 40 min
cards.body: 40 minutes on **Logical reasoning: series, coding-decoding, relations, syllogisms**. You will cover: Coding–decoding; Blood relations; Direction sense; Syllogisms (use Venn diagrams); Seating arrangement; Quick aptitude refresh (often hidden inside logic/cognitive).

cards.heading: Coding–decoding
cards.body: Letter positions: A1 B2 … Z26. Reverse: A↔Z (sum 27). Shortcut "EJOTY" = 5,10,15,20,25. If CAT → DBU (+1 each), then DOG → EPH.

cards.heading: Blood relations
cards.body: Draw a family tree: + male, − female, horizontal line = siblings/couple, vertical = generation. "Pointing to a man, Riya says, 'His mother is the only daughter of my mother.'" → only daughter of Riya's mother = Riya → Riya is his mother.

cards.heading: Direction sense
cards.body: Draw axes. Right turn from North = East. Final distance by Pythagoras (3 km and 4 km → 5 km).

cards.heading: Syllogisms (use Venn diagrams)
cards.body: "All A are B, Some B are C" → "Some A are C"? Not definitely (can't conclude). "All A are B, All B are C" → All A are C ✓. "No A is B, All C are A" → No C is B ✓.

cards.heading: Seating arrangement
cards.body: Linear or circular; fix the most definite clue first; in circles facing centre, left = clockwise.

cards.heading: Quick aptitude refresh (often hidden inside logic/cognitive)
cards.body:
- Percentage: x% of y = y% of x. Increase 20% then decrease 20% → net −4%.
- Profit% = (SP − CP)/CP × 100.
- Speed = distance/time; km/h → m/s × 5/18. Relative speed: same direction subtract, opposite add.
- Work: A in a days, B in b days → together ab/(a+b).
- Average, ratio, simple interest PRT/100, compound A = P(1+r/100)ⁿ.
- Number of handshakes among n = n(n−1)/2. Clock angle = |30H − 5.5M|.

cards.heading: Overview

cards.heading: Tailored draft (edit to your voice)
cards.body: "I'm Paikhomba, a final-year Computer Science student at SASTRA University, originally from Manipur. I build and ship full-stack products. Most recently I worked on a beauty-artist booking marketplace where I handled escrow payments, KYC verification and webhook reliability; before that I built a multi-tenant school management SaaS on GCP Cloud Run, and I was part of the core team at HYRUP, a career platform for Tier 2/3 students, where I worked on job aggregation, ranking and AI features. I also co-organised a 5-day web development bootcamp for 600+ students. I enjoy owning a feature end to end — architecture, code and production issues — and I'd like to bring that to Capgemini's client projects, especially in cloud and AI-driven engineering."

cards.heading: How to answer technical questions
cards.body:
1. Define in one line → 2. explain with an example → 3. mention a trade-off or where you used it.

"What is indexing?" → "An index is a data structure, usually a B+ tree, that lets the database find rows without scanning the table — like a book index. It speeds up reads but slows writes and takes space. In my project I added a compound index on (institution_id, created_at) because every query was scoped by tenant."

cards.heading: If you don't know
cards.body: Say so honestly, then reason aloud: "I haven't used that directly, but I think it works like… because…". Interviewers value reasoning over bluffing.

packs.title: Project deep-dive: defend every line
packs.summary: Interview lesson (40 min of study time) · Your projects — likely questions to prepare

cards.heading: Interview · 40 min
cards.body: Expect: "Explain your architecture", "Why this database?", "What was the hardest bug?", "How would you scale it 10×?", "What would you change?". Prepare each project with this frame:

cards.heading: Overview
cards.body:
- **Problem** — Who uses it, what pain it solves (1 line)
- **Architecture** — Draw it: client → API → services → DB/cache/queue → third-party. Be able to sketch in 60 s
- **Tech choices + why** — And what you'd pick otherwise ("Postgres over Mongo because relational data + transactions")
- **Your contribution** — "I" not "we" for your parts
- **Hardest problem** — Use STAR with a technical root cause
- **Numbers** — Users, requests, latency, records, time saved
- **Trade-offs & improvements** — Show maturity: what breaks at 10×, what you'd refactor

cards.heading: Inroll — multi-tenant school SaaS on GCP
cards.body:
• How is tenant data isolated (shared DB with tenant_id vs schema/DB per tenant)? Trade-offs?

• Why Cloud Run + global HTTPS load balancer? Cold starts? How does wildcard subdomain routing (∗.inroll.in) map to a tenant?

• Explain the Redis TLS newline bug and the Prisma JsonNull vs AnyNull issue — root cause and fix.

• How do you prevent one school reading another's data (every query scoped, middleware, tests)?

cards.heading: Mimora — booking marketplace with escrow + KYC
cards.body:
• Walk through the escrow payment flow: booking → payment captured → held → released on completion → refunds/disputes.

• Webhooks: how do you handle retries, duplicates (idempotency), signature verification, out-of-order events?

• KYC gate: where is it enforced (backend, not just UI)? What happens to bookings before verification?

• Data model of the Flexi booking module (4 tables) — why that design?

cards.heading: HYRUP — career platform (Node/Express, MongoDB, React, Redis, GCP)
cards.body:
• How did you aggregate jobs from 4 platforms into one model? Deduplication? Scheduling?

• Job ranking logic and leaderboard validation — how prevent cheating?

• Why MongoDB here? Where did Redis help (caching, sessions, rate limits)?

• AI features (resume rating, ATS check): prompt design, cost, hallucination handling, evaluation.

• An unauthenticated route existed — how would you audit and fix auth across routes?

packs.title: System design basics for freshers
packs.summary: Interview lesson (45 min of study time) · Framework (in this order) · Building blocks

cards.heading: Interview · 45 min
cards.body: You won't design Netflix in detail, but expect "how would you scale your project?" or "design a URL shortener / parking lot / notification system at a high level".

cards.heading: Framework (in this order)
cards.body:
1. **Clarify requirements**: functional (what it does) + non-functional (users, latency, availability, consistency).
2. **Estimate**: requests/sec, storage.
3. **API design**: key endpoints.
4. **Data model**: tables/collections.
5. **High-level diagram**.
6. **Deep-dive & bottlenecks**: scaling, caching, failures.

cards.heading: Building blocks
cards.body:
- **Load balancer** — Spread traffic across servers, health checks
- **Stateless app servers** — Easy horizontal scaling (sessions in Redis/tokens)
- **Cache (Redis) + CDN** — Fast reads, reduce DB load; cache invalidation strategy (TTL, write-through)
- **DB replication** — Primary for writes, read replicas for reads
- **Sharding / partitioning** — Split data across DBs by key (tenant_id, user_id)
- **Message queue (Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS, Pub/Sub)** — Async work (emails, notifications), decoupling, smoothing spikes
- **Rate limiter** — Protect from abuse (token bucket)
- **Monitoring & logging** — Detect and debug issues

**CAP theorem**: during a network partition you choose Consistency or Availability. Banking → consistency; social feed → availability. **Monolith vs microservices**: monolith is simpler to start; microservices scale teams/services independently but add network and ops complexity.

cards.heading: URL shortener in 6 lines
cards.body: POST /shorten {url} → generate 7-char base62 ID (counter or hash) → store (id → url) in a key-value DB. GET /{id} → look up (cache in Redis) → 301/302 redirect. Scale: read-heavy → cache + replicas; unique IDs via a distributed counter or ranges per server; analytics via a queue.

cards.heading: Exam flow (reported 2027 pattern)
cards.body:
- **1** — Stage: English LSRW (AI-scored) · Time: ~30 min · Key move: Never stay silent · chunk sentences · PREP for topics · email = subject, purpose, details, CTA, close
- **2** — Stage: Technical module: 20 AI + 20 Tech MCQs · Time: ~40–50 min · Key move: ~1 min/Q · trace tables for pseudocode · 'validate', 'human oversight' = responsible answers
- **3** — Stage: Debugging (C/C++/Java, 1 task) · Time: ~20 min · Key move: Review → Identify → Fix → Validate · boundaries, init, operators, base cases
- **4** — Stage: AI-assisted coding · Time: ~45 min · Key move: Understand → structured prompt → review every line → test edge cases
- **5** — Stage: Cognitive (Motion, Grid, Logic, Behaviour) · Time: ~20–30 min · Key move: Plan before moving · encode grid as a shape · consistent behaviour answers
- **6–7** — Stage: Technical + HR interviews · Time: 20–35 / 10–20 min · Key move: Project architecture + why · STAR stories · Capgemini values

cards.heading: Complexities
cards.body: Binary search O(log n) · merge sort O(n log n), stable, O(n) space · quick sort avg O(n log n), worst O(n²) · hash map avg O(1) · BFS/DFS O(V+E) · Dijkstra O((V+E) log V) · heap push/pop O(log n) · BST balanced O(log n), skewed O(n).

cards.heading: Numbers to remember
cards.body: int ≈ ±2.1×10⁹ · 10⁸ ops ≈ 1 s · max nodes binary tree height h = 2^(h+1)−1 · edges in tree = n−1 · complete graph edges n(n−1)/2 · Hanoi 2ⁿ−1 · /24 → 254 hosts · ports 80/443/22/53/3306 · 1 token ≈ 4 chars ≈ ¾ word.

cards.heading: One-liners
cards.body: 401 = not authenticated, 403 = not allowed · POST not idempotent · API key = app, token = user (short-lived) · JWT signed not encrypted · WHERE rows, HAVING groups · IS NULL not = NULL · DENSE_RANK no gaps · TRUNCATE (DDL) vs DELETE (DML) · Deadlock: mutual exclusion, hold & wait, no preemption, circular wait · Threads share heap, own stack · TCP reliable, UDP fast · Container shares kernel, VM has guest OS · IaaS EC2 / PaaS Cloud Run / SaaS Gmail · Product Owner owns backlog · git fetch ≠ pull · revert for shared history · parameterised queries stop SQLi · bcrypt + salt for passwords.

cards.heading: AI one-liners
cards.body: LLM = next-token predictor (Transformer, self-attention) · temperature low for code · hallucination → validate/RAG · RAG = retrieve then generate (open book) · fine-tune = change behaviour/style · embeddings + cosine similarity → semantic search · agent = plan + tools + memory loop · prompt injection = malicious instructions in data · R-C-T-C-F-E prompt: Role, Context, Task, Constraints, Format, Examples · few-shot = examples · CoT = step by step.

cards.heading: Debug scan order
cards.body: 1) loop bounds < vs <= · 2) initial values (0 vs INT_MIN, dp init) · 3) = vs ==, & vs && · 4) integer division/overflow · 5) recursion base case + return value · 6) null checks · 7) visited marking · 8) index offset i-1 · 9) missing break/return · 10) output format. React: state mutation, deps array, cleanup, keys, onClick={fn}. Java: equals, length vs length(), immutable String.

packs.title: Drill · Grammar core: tenses & subject–verb agreement (part 1/2)
packs.summary: 7 multiple-choice questions on this topic. Decide first, then reveal.

cards.heading: How to use this drill
cards.body: 7 questions from the exam-style bank on **Grammar core: tenses & subject–verb agreement**. For each one: commit to an answer first, then reveal. Count the ones you got right *before* looking.

cards.heading: Question 1
cards.body:
Q: Choose the correct sentence.

- A) I have completed the report yesterday.
- B) I completed the report yesterday.
- C) I had complete the report yesterday.
- D) I was completed the report yesterday.

A: **B) I completed the report yesterday.**

A finished time ('yesterday') takes past simple, not present perfect.

cards.heading: Question 2
cards.body:
Q: The list of pending tickets ___ growing every day.

- A) are
- B) were
- C) is
- D) have been

A: **C) is**

Subject is 'list' (singular); 'of pending tickets' is a phrase in between.

cards.heading: Question 3
cards.body:
Q: Each of the developers ___ a separate test environment.

- A) have
- B) has
- C) are having
- D) were having

A: **B) has**

'Each' is singular → 'has'.

cards.heading: Question 4
cards.body:
Q: Neither the manager nor the developers ___ aware of the change.

- A) was
- B) were
- C) is
- D) has been

A: **B) were**

With neither…nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject ('developers' → plural).

cards.heading: Question 5
cards.body:
Q: If I ___ the team lead, I would approve the leave.

- A) am
- B) was being
- C) were
- D) will be

A: **C) were**

Second conditional (imaginary present) uses 'were' for all subjects.

cards.heading: Question 6
cards.body:
Q: She ___ in this company since 2024.

- A) works
- B) is working
- C) has been working
- D) worked

A: **C) has been working**

Action started in the past and continues now with 'since' → present perfect continuous.

cards.heading: Question 7
cards.body:
Q: By the time the client called, we ___ the issue.

- A) fixed
- B) have fixed
- C) had fixed
- D) were fixing

A: **C) had fixed**

Earlier of two past actions → past perfect.

cards.heading: After the drill
cards.body: Tally your score. For every miss, name the reason — **concept gap**, **careless slip** or **time** — and fix that, not just the answer. Concept gaps send you back to “Grammar core: tenses & subject–verb agreement”.

packs.title: Drill · Grammar core: tenses & subject–verb agreement (part 2/2)
packs.summary: 7 multiple-choice questions on this topic. Decide first, then reveal.

cards.heading: How to use this drill
cards.body: 7 questions from the exam-style bank on **Grammar core: tenses & subject–verb agreement**. For each one: commit to an answer first, then reveal. Count the ones you got right *before* looking.

cards.heading: Question 8
cards.body:
Q: If the build ___ , we will release tonight.

- A) will pass
- B) passes
- C) passed
- D) would pass

A: **B) passes**

First conditional: present simple in the if-clause, will in the main clause.

cards.heading: Question 9
cards.body:
Q: Which sentence is in the passive voice?

- A) The tester found three bugs.
- B) Three bugs were found by the tester.
- C) The tester is finding bugs.
- D) The tester has found bugs.

A: **B) Three bugs were found by the tester.**

Passive = be + past participle; the object becomes the subject.

cards.heading: Question 10
cards.body:
Q: He said, 'I am working on the API.' → Reported speech:

- A) He said that he is working on the API.
- B) He said that he was working on the API.
- C) He said that I was working on the API.
- D) He said he has been working on the API.

A: **B) He said that he was working on the API.**

Shift present continuous back to past continuous and change the pronoun.

cards.heading: Question 11
cards.body:
Q: I ___ the answer to your question.

- A) am knowing
- B) know
- C) knowing
- D) am know

A: **B) know**

'Know' is a stative verb; not used in continuous form.

cards.heading: Question 12
cards.body:
Q: The manager, along with his team members, ___ attending the conference.

- A) are
- B) is
- C) were
- D) have been

A: **B) is**

'Along with' does not change the subject; 'manager' is singular.

cards.heading: Question 13
cards.body:
Q: If we had tested the module properly, we ___ the bug earlier.

- A) would catch
- B) will catch
- C) would have caught
- D) had caught

A: **C) would have caught**

Third conditional: had + V3 → would have + V3.

cards.heading: Question 14
cards.body:
Q: The team ___ deciding on the new framework today.

- A) are
- B) is
- C) have
- D) be

A: **B) is**

Collective noun acting as one unit → singular verb (standard in tests).

cards.heading: After the drill
cards.body: Tally your score. For every miss, name the reason — **concept gap**, **careless slip** or **time** — and fix that, not just the answer. Concept gaps send you back to “Grammar core: tenses & subject–verb agreement”.

packs.title: Drill · Articles, prepositions & Indian-English errors (part 1/2)
packs.summary: 7 multiple-choice questions on this topic. Decide first, then reveal.

cards.heading: How to use this drill
cards.body: 7 questions from the exam-style bank on **Articles, prepositions & Indian-English errors**. For each one: commit to an answer first, then reveal. Count the ones you got right *before* looking.

cards.heading: Question 1
cards.body:
Q: Choose the correct option: She has ___ MBA from ___ reputed university.

- A) a, an
- B) an, a
- C) an, an
- D) a, a

A: **B) an, a**

'MBA' begins with a vowel sound (em) → an; 'university' begins with a 'yoo' sound → a.

cards.heading: Question 2
cards.body:
Q: We need to discuss ___ the deployment plan.

- A) about
- B) on
- C) over
- D) no preposition

A: **D) no preposition**

'Discuss' is transitive — no preposition: 'discuss the plan'.

cards.heading: Question 3
cards.body:
Q: The system ___ five microservices.

- A) comprises of
- B) comprises
- C) is comprising of
- D) comprise of

A: **B) comprises**

'Comprise' takes no 'of'. ('consists of' is correct.)

cards.heading: Question 4
cards.body:
Q: Which is the most professional replacement for 'Kindly do the needful'?

- A) Do it fast.
- B) Please do needful at the earliest.
- C) Could you please share the updated invoice by Friday?
- D) Revert back ASAP.

A: **C) Could you please share the updated invoice by Friday?**

Specific, polite, with a clear action and deadline.

cards.heading: Question 5
cards.body:
Q: I have been working here ___ two years.

- A) since
- B) for
- C) from
- D) by

A: **B) for**

'For' + duration; 'since' + point in time.

cards.heading: Question 6
cards.body:
Q: The meeting is scheduled ___ Monday ___ 10 am.

- A) in, at
- B) on, at
- C) at, on
- D) on, in

A: **B) on, at**

on + day, at + clock time.

cards.heading: Question 7
cards.body:
Q: Select the correct sentence.

- A) One of my friend works at Capgemini.
- B) One of my friends work at Capgemini.
- C) One of my friends works at Capgemini.
- D) One of my friends are working at Capgemini.

A: **C) One of my friends works at Capgemini.**

'One of' + plural noun, but the verb agrees with 'one' (singular).

cards.heading: After the drill
cards.body: Tally your score. For every miss, name the reason — **concept gap**, **careless slip** or **time** — and fix that, not just the answer. Concept gaps send you back to “Articles, prepositions & Indian-English errors”.

packs.title: Drill · Articles, prepositions & Indian-English errors (part 2/2)
packs.summary: 7 multiple-choice questions on this topic. Decide first, then reveal.

cards.heading: How to use this drill
cards.body: 7 questions from the exam-style bank on **Articles, prepositions & Indian-English errors**. For each one: commit to an answer first, then reveal. Count the ones you got right *before* looking.

cards.heading: Question 8
cards.body:
Q: Please reply ___ this email by noon.

- A) back
- B) to
- C) for
- D) on

A: **B) to**

'Reply to' something.

cards.heading: Question 9
cards.body:
Q: The new policy will ___ all employees from next month.

- A) effect
- B) affect
- C) effects
- D) affection

A: **B) affect**

'Affect' is the verb meaning to influence.

cards.heading: Question 10
cards.body:
Q: ___ important to back up the database before migration.

- A) Its
- B) It's
- C) Its'
- D) It

A: **B) It's**

It's = it is.

cards.heading: Question 11
cards.body:
Q: There were ___ errors in this release than in the last one.

- A) less
- B) lesser
- C) fewer
- D) little

A: **C) fewer**

Errors are countable → fewer.

cards.heading: Question 12
cards.body:
Q: To ___ shall I address the escalation?

- A) who
- B) whom
- C) whose
- D) which

A: **B) whom**

Object of a preposition → whom (test: 'address it to him').

cards.heading: Question 13
cards.body:
Q: He is very good ___ explaining complex topics.

- A) in
- B) at
- C) on
- D) with

A: **B) at**

Collocation: good at.

cards.heading: Question 14
cards.body:
Q: Spot the error: 'Please revert back to me with your feedback.'

- A) Please
- B) revert back
- C) to me
- D) with your feedback

A: **B) revert back**

'Revert back' is redundant/Indian-English; use 'reply to me' or 'get back to me'.

cards.heading: After the drill
cards.body: Tally your score. For every miss, name the reason — **concept gap**, **careless slip** or **time** — and fix that, not just the answer. Concept gaps send you back to “Articles, prepositions & Indian-English errors”.

packs.title: Drill · Sentence completion, correction & vocabulary (part 1/2)
packs.summary: 7 multiple-choice questions on this topic. Decide first, then reveal.

cards.heading: How to use this drill
cards.body: 7 questions from the exam-style bank on **Sentence completion, correction & vocabulary**. For each one: commit to an answer first, then reveal. Count the ones you got right *before* looking.

cards.heading: Question 1
cards.body:
Q: Although the deadline was tight, the team ___ the release on time.

- A) missed
- B) delivered
- C) postponed
- D) cancelled

A: **B) delivered**

'Although' signals contrast with 'tight deadline' → positive outcome.

cards.heading: Question 2
cards.body:
Q: Choose the word closest in meaning to MITIGATE.

- A) worsen
- B) reduce
- C) ignore
- D) measure

A: **B) reduce**

Mitigate = make less severe.

cards.heading: Question 3
cards.body:
Q: Choose the antonym of OBSOLETE.

- A) outdated
- B) ancient
- C) modern
- D) useless

A: **C) modern**

Obsolete = no longer used; opposite = modern/current.

cards.heading: Question 4
cards.body:
Q: We need to ___ a decision before the client meeting.

- A) do
- B) make
- C) take up
- D) give

A: **B) make**

Collocation: make a decision.

cards.heading: Question 5
cards.body:
Q: The requirements were ___, so the team asked the client for clarification.

- A) ambiguous
- B) lucid
- C) concise
- D) obvious

A: **A) ambiguous**

Unclear requirements lead to clarification → ambiguous.

cards.heading: Question 6
cards.body:
Q: Our server costs rose sharply; ___, we moved to auto-scaling.

- A) however
- B) therefore
- C) although
- D) unless

A: **B) therefore**

Cause → result: therefore.

cards.heading: Question 7
cards.body:
Q: Synonym of EXPEDITE:

- A) delay
- B) speed up
- C) explain
- D) examine

A: **B) speed up**

Expedite = make happen faster.

cards.heading: After the drill
cards.body: Tally your score. For every miss, name the reason — **concept gap**, **careless slip** or **time** — and fix that, not just the answer. Concept gaps send you back to “Sentence completion, correction & vocabulary”.

packs.title: Drill · Sentence completion, correction & vocabulary (part 2/2)
packs.summary: 6 multiple-choice questions on this topic. Decide first, then reveal.

cards.heading: How to use this drill
cards.body: 6 questions from the exam-style bank on **Sentence completion, correction & vocabulary**. For each one: commit to an answer first, then reveal. Count the ones you got right *before* looking.

cards.heading: Question 8
cards.body:
Q: Synonym of CANDID:

- A) frank
- B) secretive
- C) careful
- D) polite

A: **A) frank**

Candid = honest and direct.

cards.heading: Question 9
cards.body:
Q: Arrange into a sentence: (P) has been approved (Q) for the new project (R) the budget (S) by the finance team

- A) RQPS
- B) PRQS
- C) RPQS
- D) QRSP

A: **A) RQPS**

Subject phrase first: 'The budget for the new project (R+Q) has been approved (P) by the finance team (S).'

cards.heading: Question 10
cards.body:
Q: She explained the architecture so ___ that even new interns understood it.

- A) clear
- B) clearly
- C) clearer
- D) clarity

A: **B) clearly**

Modifies the verb 'explained' → adverb 'clearly'.

cards.heading: Question 11
cards.body:
Q: The word 'tentative' in 'a tentative release date' means:

- A) final
- B) not yet confirmed
- C) delayed
- D) early

A: **B) not yet confirmed**

Tentative = provisional, may change.

cards.heading: Question 12
cards.body:
Q: Choose the correctly spelt word.

- A) Accomodate
- B) Acommodate
- C) Accommodate
- D) Acomodate

A: **C) Accommodate**

Double c, double m.

cards.heading: Question 13
cards.body:
Q: He is ___ to take on new responsibilities; he volunteers for every task.

- A) reluctant
- B) eager
- C) hesitant
- D) unwilling

A: **B) eager**

Volunteering shows eagerness.

packs.title: Drill · Reading comprehension: a 4-step method
packs.summary: 5 multiple-choice questions on this topic. Decide first, then reveal.

cards.heading: How to use this drill
cards.body: 5 questions from the exam-style bank on **Reading comprehension: a 4-step method**. For each one: commit to an answer first, then reveal. Count the ones you got right *before* looking.

cards.heading: Question 1
cards.body:
Q: Passage: 'Moving the billing system to the cloud cut infrastructure costs by 30%, although the operations team needed three months of retraining.' Which statement is best supported?

- A) The operations team disliked the cloud.
- B) The migration had a cost benefit and a short-term training cost.
- C) Infrastructure costs doubled.
- D) Training was unnecessary.

A: **B) The migration had a cost benefit and a short-term training cost.**

Only this is directly supported; the others are unstated or contradicted.

cards.heading: Question 2
cards.body:
Q: Passage: 'Automated tests catch regressions early, but they cannot replace exploratory testing, which uncovers issues no one thought to script.' The author's view is that:

- A) Automated testing is useless.
- B) Exploratory testing should replace automation.
- C) Both automated and exploratory testing have a role.
- D) Regressions are rare.

A: **C) Both automated and exploratory testing have a role.**

The 'but' sentence balances both methods.

cards.heading: Question 3
cards.body:
Q: In a passage, 'The startup's growth was meteoric' — 'meteoric' most nearly means:

- A) slow
- B) sudden and rapid
- C) dangerous
- D) temporary

A: **B) sudden and rapid**

Meteoric = very rapid success.

cards.heading: Question 4
cards.body:
Q: Which option is usually a TRAP in reading comprehension?

- A) A paraphrase of a line
- B) An option with 'always' or 'never' not stated in the passage
- C) An option matching the main idea
- D) An option supported by two lines

A: **B) An option with 'always' or 'never' not stated in the passage**

Extreme words are usually unsupported.

cards.heading: Question 5
cards.body:
Q: Passage: 'Remote onboarding reduced travel costs, yet new hires reported feeling disconnected for their first month.' The best title is:

- A) The Cost of Travel
- B) Remote Onboarding: Savings and Social Challenges
- C) Why New Hires Quit
- D) Travel Policies in IT

A: **B) Remote Onboarding: Savings and Social Challenges**

Covers both halves of the passage — not too narrow, not too broad.

cards.heading: After the drill
cards.body: Tally your score. For every miss, name the reason — **concept gap**, **careless slip** or **time** — and fix that, not just the answer. Concept gaps send you back to “Reading comprehension: a 4-step method”.

packs.title: Drill · Listening, repeat & dictation technique
packs.summary: 3 multiple-choice questions on this topic. Decide first, then reveal.

cards.heading: How to use this drill
cards.body: 3 questions from the exam-style bank on **Listening, repeat & dictation technique**. For each one: commit to an answer first, then reveal. Count the ones you got right *before* looking.

cards.heading: Question 1
cards.body:
Q: In a listen-and-repeat task, the best strategy is to:

- A) memorise each word individually
- B) remember chunks of meaning and start speaking immediately
- C) wait 5 seconds to think
- D) write the sentence down first

A: **B) remember chunks of meaning and start speaking immediately**

Chunking + immediate response preserves short-term memory.

cards.heading: Question 2
cards.body:
Q: In dictation, the most common errors are:

- A) capital letters
- B) plural -s and past tense -ed endings
- C) long words
- D) proper nouns

A: **B) plural -s and past tense -ed endings**

Small endings are easily missed when listening.

cards.heading: Question 3
cards.body:
Q: If you forget the end of a sentence in a repeat task, you should:

- A) stay silent
- B) say 'sorry'
- C) say confidently what you remember
- D) repeat the first word several times

A: **C) say confidently what you remember**

Partial answers earn partial credit; silence earns none.

cards.heading: After the drill
cards.body: Tally your score. For every miss, name the reason — **concept gap**, **careless slip** or **time** — and fix that, not just the answer. Concept gaps send you back to “Listening, repeat & dictation technique”.

packs.title: Drill · Speaking: read-aloud and the 60-second topic
packs.summary: 5 multiple-choice questions on this topic. Decide first, then reveal.

cards.heading: How to use this drill
cards.body: 5 questions from the exam-style bank on **Speaking: read-aloud and the 60-second topic**. For each one: commit to an answer first, then reveal. Count the ones you got right *before* looking.

cards.heading: Question 1
cards.body:
Q: Which structure fits a 60-second opinion topic best?

- A) Point – Reason – Example – Point
- B) Example only
- C) List of facts
- D) Question – Question – Answer

A: **A) Point – Reason – Example – Point**

PREP gives a clear, complete answer within time.

cards.heading: Question 2
cards.body:
Q: An ideal speaking pace for AI-scored tests is about:

- A) 70–90 words per minute
- B) 130–150 words per minute
- C) 200–220 words per minute
- D) as fast as possible

A: **B) 130–150 words per minute**

Natural conversational pace is scored best for fluency.

cards.heading: Question 3
cards.body:
Q: For 'Describe a time you solved a problem in a team', the best framework is:

- A) SWOT
- B) STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result)
- C) 5W1H
- D) PESTLE

A: **B) STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result)**

STAR is designed for experience-based questions.

cards.heading: Question 4
cards.body:
Q: Which hurts your fluency score most?

- A) A short pause between ideas
- B) Frequent fillers like 'umm', 'like', 'basically'
- C) Using simple vocabulary
- D) Speaking in a neutral accent

A: **B) Frequent fillers like 'umm', 'like', 'basically'**

Fillers and restarts break fluency; short pauses are fine.

cards.heading: Question 5
cards.body:
Q: In read-aloud, you should pause longer at:

- A) every word
- B) commas
- C) full stops
- D) every line break

A: **C) full stops**

Full stop = longer pause; comma = short pause.

cards.heading: After the drill
cards.body: Tally your score. For every miss, name the reason — **concept gap**, **careless slip** or **time** — and fix that, not just the answer. Concept gaps send you back to “Speaking: read-aloud and the 60-second topic”.

packs.title: Drill · Business email writing: the template that always works
packs.summary: 6 multiple-choice questions on this topic. Decide first, then reveal.

cards.heading: How to use this drill
cards.body: 6 questions from the exam-style bank on **Business email writing: the template that always works**. For each one: commit to an answer first, then reveal. Count the ones you got right *before* looking.

cards.heading: Question 1
cards.body:
Q: Which is the best subject line for informing a client about an outage?

- A) Hi
- B) Problem
- C) Payment service outage on 12 June – resolved, root cause inside
- D) URGENT!!! READ NOW

A: **C) Payment service outage on 12 June – resolved, root cause inside**

Specific, informative, professional.

cards.heading: Question 2
cards.body:
Q: Which is the best opening line of a delay email to a client?

- A) Sorry we are late as usual.
- B) I am writing to inform you that the UAT build will move from 10 June to 14 June.
- C) Hope you are doing great and enjoying the weather!!
- D) As you know, delays happen.

A: **B) I am writing to inform you that the UAT build will move from 10 June to 14 June.**

States the purpose clearly in the first line.

cards.heading: Question 3
cards.body:
Q: Which is the best call to action?

- A) Let me know.
- B) Waiting for reply.
- C) Could you please confirm by Thursday 5 pm whether the revised date works for you?
- D) Do the needful.

A: **C) Could you please confirm by Thursday 5 pm whether the revised date works for you?**

Specific action and deadline.

cards.heading: Question 4
cards.body:
Q: The most appropriate closing for a formal client email is:

- A) Cheers!!
- B) Bye
- C) Best regards,
- D) Ur friend,

A: **C) Best regards,**

Standard professional sign-off.

cards.heading: Question 5
cards.body:
Q: Which sentence keeps a professional tone when declining a request?

- A) That's not my job.
- B) Thank you for reaching out; unfortunately, we cannot add this feature in the current sprint, but we can plan it for the next one.
- C) No.
- D) Why are you asking this now?

A: **B) Thank you for reaching out; unfortunately, we cannot add this feature in the current sprint, but we can plan it for the next one.**

Polite, explains, offers an alternative.

cards.heading: Question 6
cards.body:
Q: An outage email should NOT include:

- A) the impact
- B) the ETA for the fix
- C) the name of the junior engineer who caused it
- D) preventive steps

A: **C) the name of the junior engineer who caused it**

Never blame individuals in client communication.

cards.heading: After the drill
cards.body: Tally your score. For every miss, name the reason — **concept gap**, **careless slip** or **time** — and fix that, not just the answer. Concept gaps send you back to “Business email writing: the template that always works”.

packs.title: Drill · Situational awareness: handling client scenarios (SJT)
packs.summary: 6 multiple-choice questions on this topic. Decide first, then reveal.

cards.heading: How to use this drill
cards.body: 6 questions from the exam-style bank on **Situational awareness: handling client scenarios (SJT)**. For each one: commit to an answer first, then reveal. Count the ones you got right *before* looking.

cards.heading: Question 1
cards.body:
Q: You realise the code you deployed yesterday has a bug affecting some users. Best action?

- A) Wait and hope no one notices.
- B) Inform your lead immediately with details and a proposed fix/rollback.
- C) Fix it silently without telling anyone.
- D) Blame the tester for missing it.

A: **B) Inform your lead immediately with details and a proposed fix/rollback.**

Honesty and ownership with a solution.

cards.heading: Question 2
cards.body:
Q: A client asks for a delivery date you know is unrealistic. Best response?

- A) Agree to keep them happy.
- B) Explain the constraints honestly and propose a realistic date or a phased delivery.
- C) Ignore the request.
- D) Tell them it's impossible without explanation.

A: **B) Explain the constraints honestly and propose a realistic date or a phased delivery.**

Transparent and solution-focused.

cards.heading: Question 3
cards.body:
Q: A teammate repeatedly misses stand-ups, delaying your work. First step?

- A) Complain to HR.
- B) Talk to the teammate privately to understand and agree on a solution.
- C) Ignore it.
- D) Post about it in the team chat.

A: **B) Talk to the teammate privately to understand and agree on a solution.**

Address directly and respectfully first; escalate only if needed.

cards.heading: Question 4
cards.body:
Q: During a client call you are asked a technical question you can't answer. Best response?

- A) Make up an answer.
- B) Say you'll confirm and get back by a specific time, then follow up.
- C) Stay silent.
- D) Say it's not your area.

A: **B) Say you'll confirm and get back by a specific time, then follow up.**

Honest, accountable, committed follow-up.

cards.heading: Question 5
cards.body:
Q: A client shares confidential production data on a public chat channel by mistake. You should:

- A) Ignore it.
- B) Alert them politely and follow the data-handling/security process to remove it.
- C) Download it for later use.
- D) Forward it to your team.

A: **B) Alert them politely and follow the data-handling/security process to remove it.**

Protect confidentiality and follow procedure.

cards.heading: Question 6
cards.body:
Q: You finish your sprint tasks two days early. Best action?

- A) Relax until the sprint ends.
- B) Inform the Scrum Master/lead and offer to help others or pick up backlog items.
- C) Start a personal side project at work.
- D) Hide it so you're not given more work.

A: **B) Inform the Scrum Master/lead and offer to help others or pick up backlog items.**

Team spirit and proactiveness.

cards.heading: After the drill
cards.body: Tally your score. For every miss, name the reason — **concept gap**, **careless slip** or **time** — and fix that, not just the answer. Concept gaps send you back to “Situational awareness: handling client scenarios (SJT)”.

packs.title: Drill · AI, ML, Deep Learning & GenAI — the family tree
packs.summary: 8 multiple-choice questions on this topic. Decide first, then reveal.

cards.heading: How to use this drill
cards.body: 8 questions from the exam-style bank on **AI, ML, Deep Learning & GenAI — the family tree**. For each one: commit to an answer first, then reveal. Count the ones you got right *before* looking.

cards.heading: Question 1
cards.body:
Q: Which is the correct hierarchy?

- A) GenAI ⊃ ML ⊃ AI
- B) AI ⊃ ML ⊃ Deep Learning ⊃ GenAI
- C) ML ⊃ AI ⊃ GenAI
- D) Deep Learning ⊃ AI ⊃ ML

A: **B) AI ⊃ ML ⊃ Deep Learning ⊃ GenAI**

AI is the broadest; GenAI is a subset of deep learning.

cards.heading: Question 2
cards.body:
Q: A model trained on emails labelled 'spam' or 'not spam' is an example of:

- A) Unsupervised learning
- B) Supervised learning (classification)
- C) Reinforcement learning
- D) Clustering

A: **B) Supervised learning (classification)**

Labelled data with categories → supervised classification.

cards.heading: Question 3
cards.body:
Q: Grouping customers into segments without predefined labels is:

- A) Regression
- B) Classification
- C) Clustering (unsupervised)
- D) Reinforcement learning

A: **C) Clustering (unsupervised)**

No labels, finding structure → clustering.

cards.heading: Question 4
cards.body:
Q: An agent learning to play a game by receiving rewards and penalties uses:

- A) Supervised learning
- B) Reinforcement learning
- C) Unsupervised learning
- D) Transfer learning

A: **B) Reinforcement learning**

Trial-and-error with rewards = RL.

cards.heading: Question 5
cards.body:
Q: A model scores 99% on training data but 60% on new data. This is:

- A) Underfitting
- B) Overfitting
- C) Good generalisation
- D) Data augmentation

A: **B) Overfitting**

Memorised training data; fails to generalise.

cards.heading: Question 6
cards.body:
Q: Predicting a house's price (a continuous number) is a:

- A) Classification task
- B) Regression task
- C) Clustering task
- D) Ranking task

A: **B) Regression task**

Continuous output → regression.

cards.heading: Question 7
cards.body:
Q: 'Inference' in machine learning means:

- A) training the model
- B) using a trained model to make predictions
- C) collecting data
- D) labelling data

A: **B) using a trained model to make predictions**

Inference = applying the trained model.

cards.heading: Question 8
cards.body:
Q: RLHF stands for:

- A) Recursive Learning for High Frequency
- B) Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
- C) Random Labelling with Human Filters
- D) Regression Learning with Hidden Features

A: **B) Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback**

Used to align chatbots with human preferences.

cards.body: Tally your score. For every miss, name the reason — **concept gap**, **careless slip** or **time** — and fix that, not just the answer. Concept gaps send you back to “AI, ML, Deep Learning & GenAI — the family tree”.

packs.title: Drill · How LLMs work: tokens, context, temperature (part 1/2)
packs.summary: 6 multiple-choice questions on this topic. Decide first, then reveal.

cards.heading: How to use this drill
cards.body: 6 questions from the exam-style bank on **How LLMs work: tokens, context, temperature**. For each one: commit to an answer first, then reveal. Count the ones you got right *before* looking.

cards.heading: Question 1
cards.body:
Q: At its core, an LLM generates text by:

- A) searching the internet for answers
- B) predicting the next token repeatedly
- C) retrieving stored sentences
- D) running a rule engine

A: **B) predicting the next token repeatedly**

LLMs are next-token predictors.

cards.heading: Question 2
cards.body:
Q: Roughly how many tokens is a 750-word English text?

- A) about 100
- B) about 500
- C) about 1,000
- D) about 5,000

A: **C) about 1,000**

1 token ≈ ¾ word → 750 words ≈ 1,000 tokens.

cards.heading: Question 3
cards.body:
Q: The 'context window' of an LLM is:

- A) the UI chat window
- B) the maximum number of tokens the model can consider at once
- C) the training dataset size
- D) the time limit for a response

A: **B) the maximum number of tokens the model can consider at once**

Prompt + history + output must fit in it.

cards.heading: Question 4
cards.body:
Q: For generating deterministic, accurate code you should set temperature to:

- A) high (1.0+)
- B) low (around 0–0.2)
- C) exactly 0.5 always
- D) temperature doesn't matter

A: **B) low (around 0–0.2)**

Lower temperature = less randomness.

cards.heading: Question 5
cards.body:
Q: Which architecture underlies most modern LLMs?

- A) Convolutional Neural Network
- B) Transformer
- C) Decision tree
- D) Recurrent rule engine

A: **B) Transformer**

Transformers with self-attention.

cards.heading: Question 6
cards.body:
Q: A 'foundation model' is:

- A) a model trained for one narrow task only
- B) a large model pre-trained on broad data that can be adapted to many tasks
- C) a database schema
- D) a rule-based expert system

A: **B) a large model pre-trained on broad data that can be adapted to many tasks**

Base model adaptable via prompting/fine-tuning.

cards.heading: After the drill
cards.body: Tally your score. For every miss, name the reason — **concept gap**, **careless slip** or **time** — and fix that, not just the answer. Concept gaps send you back to “How LLMs work: tokens, context, temperature”.

packs.title: Drill · How LLMs work: tokens, context, temperature (part 2/2)
packs.summary: 5 multiple-choice questions on this topic. Decide first, then reveal.

cards.heading: How to use this drill
cards.body: 5 questions from the exam-style bank on **How LLMs work: tokens, context, temperature**. For each one: commit to an answer first, then reveal. Count the ones you got right *before* looking.

cards.heading: Question 7
cards.body:
Q: Fine-tuning means:

- A) writing longer prompts
- B) further training a pre-trained model on specific data
- C) increasing temperature
- D) adding a vector database

A: **B) further training a pre-trained model on specific data**

Adjusts the model's weights for a task/domain.

cards.heading: Question 8
cards.body:
Q: The self-attention mechanism helps a model to:

- A) store files
- B) decide which other tokens in the input are relevant to each token
- C) reduce electricity use
- D) encrypt data

A: **B) decide which other tokens in the input are relevant to each token**

Each token weighs others to build context.

cards.heading: Question 9
cards.body:
Q: A model that accepts both images and text as input is called:

- A) multimodal
- B) multitenant
- C) monolithic
- D) multithreaded

A: **A) multimodal**

Multimodal = multiple input/output types.

cards.heading: Question 10
cards.body:
Q: Top-p (nucleus) sampling controls:

- A) the context window
- B) sampling only from the most probable tokens whose cumulative probability is p
- C) training speed
- D) number of GPUs

A: **B) sampling only from the most probable tokens whose cumulative probability is p**

Another randomness control.

cards.heading: Question 11
cards.body:
Q: A 'system prompt' is:

- A) the operating system's terminal
- B) instructions that set the model's role and behaviour for the conversation
- C) the user's last message
- D) the model's training data

A: **B) instructions that set the model's role and behaviour for the conversation**

Sets persistent behaviour and rules.
