packs.title: Interview · DSA
packs.summary: 8 likely interview questions with crisp model answers.

cards.heading: How to use these
cards.body: Answer each question *aloud* in 30–45 seconds before you reveal. Interviewers want a definition, one example and one trade-off — in that order.

cards.heading: DSA · 1
cards.body:
Q: Array vs linked list?

A: Array: contiguous, O(1) index, costly middle inserts. Linked list: O(1) insert/delete at a known node, O(n) access, extra pointer memory.

cards.heading: DSA · 2
cards.body:
Q: Stack vs queue with real examples?

A: Stack LIFO (undo, call stack, browser back). Queue FIFO (printer jobs, BFS, request handling).

cards.heading: DSA · 3
cards.body:
Q: How does a hash map work?

A: Hash function maps a key to a bucket index; collisions handled by chaining or probing; average O(1) operations; resize when load factor grows.

cards.heading: DSA · 4
cards.body:
Q: When is binary search applicable?

A: On sorted (or monotonic) data; halves the search space each step, O(log n).

cards.heading: DSA · 5
cards.body:
Q: Explain merge sort vs quick sort.

A: Merge: divide, sort halves, merge — O(n log n) always, stable, O(n) space. Quick: partition around a pivot — O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst, in-place.

cards.heading: DSA · 6
cards.body:
Q: BFS vs DFS?

A: BFS uses a queue, explores level by level, finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs. DFS uses a stack/recursion, goes deep, used for cycles, topological sort.

cards.heading: DSA · 7
cards.body:
Q: What is dynamic programming?

A: Solving problems with overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure by storing sub-results (memoisation or tabulation).

cards.heading: DSA · 8
cards.body:
Q: Time complexity of common operations in a balanced BST?

A: Search, insert, delete: O(log n); inorder traversal gives sorted order.

packs.title: AI-assisted coding · Remove duplicates, keep order
packs.summary: A 20-minute walk-through of the whole round: understand, prompt, review, test.

cards.heading: 20 minutes
cards.body:
Given an array of integers (n ≤ 10⁵, values may be negative), return a new array with duplicates removed, keeping the FIRST occurrence order. Language: Java. Signature: int[] dedupe(int[] a).

The round is graded on your process — understanding, prompting, reviewing the AI's output, and testing — not just the final code.

cards.heading: Step 1
cards.body:
Q: Understand: which approach meets the constraints best?

- A) Nested loops comparing every pair (O(n²))
- B) Sort then remove adjacent duplicates
- C) One pass with a HashSet of seen values and an output list (O(n))
- D) Convert to TreeSet

A: **C) One pass with a HashSet of seen values and an output list (O(n))**

HashSet gives O(1) checks and preserves order because we append on first sight. Sorting/TreeSet destroy original order.

cards.heading: Step 2
cards.body:
Q: Write the prompt you would give the AI.

A: ```
You are an expert Java 17 developer. Implement int[] dedupe(int[] a) that removes duplicates while keeping the first-occurrence order. Use a HashSet<Integer> for seen values and an ArrayList for output; O(n) time. Handle empty array (return empty), all duplicates, negatives. Return only the code with comments, then 4 test cases with expected output.
```

Strong prompts cover: role / expertise; language / version / environment; interface: function signature / inputs & outputs; constraints; edge cases named explicitly; output format specified; ask for tests / validation.

cards.heading: Step 4
cards.body:
Q: The AI returned this. Click the line(s) with a problem.

A: **line 4: `for (int i = 0; i <= a.length; i++) {`**

i <= a.length reads one past the end → ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. Should be i < a.length. Everything else matches the spec.

cards.heading: Step 5
cards.body:
Q: Validate: pick ALL useful test inputs. (choose all that apply)

- A) [] → []
- B) [1, 2, 2, 3, 1] → [1, 2, 3]
- C) [-1, -1, 0] → [-1, 0]
- D) [5] → [5]
- E) [1, 2, 3] → [3, 2, 1]

A: **A) [] → [] and B) [1, 2, 2, 3, 1] → [1, 2, 3] and C) [-1, -1, 0] → [-1, 0] and D) [5] → [5]**

Option 5's expected output is wrong (order must be preserved). The others cover empty, mixed, negatives and single element.

cards.heading: The workflow
cards.body: Understand the problem → write a precise prompt → read what comes back → review it line by line → test the edge cases. Never accept AI output you have not run or traced.

packs.title: AI-assisted coding · Valid parentheses
packs.summary: A 20-minute walk-through of the whole round: understand, prompt, review, test.

cards.heading: 20 minutes
cards.body:
Given a string of '(', ')', '{', '}', '[' and ']' (length ≤ 10⁴), return true if brackets are balanced and properly nested. Language: C++. Signature: bool isValid(string s).

The round is graded on your process — understanding, prompting, reviewing the AI's output, and testing — not just the final code.

cards.heading: Step 1
cards.body:
Q: Which data structure fits?

- A) Queue
- B) Stack
- C) Hash set only
- D) Two counters

A: **B) Stack**

Last opened must close first → LIFO. Counters fail on '([)]'.

cards.heading: Step 2
cards.body:
Q: Write the prompt.

A: ```
You are a C++17 expert. Implement bool isValid(string s) checking balanced and properly nested (), {}, []. Use a std::stack<char> and an unordered_map from closer to opener; O(n) time. Edge cases: empty string → true, single char → false, closer first ')(' → false, '([)]' → false. Return only code with comments plus 5 test cases.
```

Strong prompts cover: role / expertise; language / version / environment; interface: function signature / inputs & outputs; constraints; edge cases named explicitly; output format specified; ask for tests / validation.

cards.heading: Step 4
cards.body:
Q: Review the AI's code. Click the problem line(s).

A: **line 7: `if (st.top() != match[c]) return false;`; line 11: `return true;`**

st.top() on an empty stack is undefined behaviour (input ')' crashes) → check st.empty() first. Final return must be st.empty(), otherwise '((' returns true.

cards.heading: Step 5
cards.body:
Q: Which tests would catch the bugs above? (choose all that apply)

- A) "()" → true
- B) ")" → false
- C) "((" → false
- D) "{[]}" → true
- E) "([)]" → false

A: **B) ")" → false and C) "((" → false**

')' hits the empty-stack top; '((' exposes the missing final empty check. The others pass even with the bugs (still good to run).

cards.heading: The workflow
cards.body: Understand the problem → write a precise prompt → read what comes back → review it line by line → test the edge cases. Never accept AI output you have not run or traced.

- A) Store a filtered copy in state and sync it in useEffect
- B) Derive it during render from users + search state (optionally useMemo)
- C) Mutate the users prop
- D) Query the DOM

cards.heading: Step 2

```
You are a React 18 expert. Modify UserList below (props: users [{id, name}]) to add a controlled search input filtering by name, case-insensitive, trimming whitespace. Return the full component in one code block, then 3 RTL tests.
```

Strong prompts cover: role / expertise; language / version / environment; clear task verb; constraints; edge cases named explicitly; output format specified.

cards.heading: Step 4
cards.body:
Q: Review. Click the problem line(s). A: **line 3: `const shown = users.filter(u => u.name.includes(q));`; line 6: ``; line 8: `
    {shown.map((u, i) =>
  • {u.name}
    • )}
`** includes(q) is case-sensitive (use toLowerCase on both). The input has value but no onChange → read-only. key={i} (index) breaks identity when the list is filtered; use u.id.

cards.heading: Step 5

packs.title: AI-assisted coding · Longest substring without repeating characters
packs.summary: A 25-minute walk-through of the whole round: understand, prompt, review, test.

cards.heading: 25 minutes
cards.body:
Given a string s (length ≤ 10⁵, ASCII), return the length of the longest substring without repeating characters. Language: Java. Signature: int longest(String s).

The round is graded on your process — understanding, prompting, reviewing the AI's output, and testing — not just the final code.

cards.heading: Step 1
cards.body:
Q: Best approach?

- A) Check all substrings O(n³)
- B) Sliding window with last-seen index map O(n)
- C) Sort the string
- D) Binary search on answer with DP

A: **B) Sliding window with last-seen index map O(n)**

Expand right; when a repeat is inside the window, jump left past its last index.

cards.heading: Step 2
cards.body:
Q: Write the prompt.

A: ```
You are a Java expert. Implement int longest(String s) returning the length of the longest substring without repeating characters. First explain the sliding-window approach in 3 lines, then code it with an int[128] last-seen array, O(n) time, O(1) space. Edge cases: empty string → 0, all same chars 'bbbb' → 1, 'abba' → 2 (left pointer must never move backwards). Return code + 5 test cases with expected output.
```

Strong prompts cover: role / expertise; language / version / environment; interface: function signature / inputs & outputs; constraints; edge cases named explicitly; output format specified; ask for tests / validation; plan / step-by-step / approach first.

cards.heading: Step 4
cards.body:
Q: Review. Click the problem line(s).

A: **line 7: `if (last[c] != -1) left = last[c] + 1;`; line 9: `best = Math.max(best, r - left);`**

left must only move forward: left = Math.max(left, last[c] + 1) (fails on 'abba'). Window length is r - left + 1.

cards.heading: Step 5
cards.body:
Q: Which inputs expose the bugs? (choose all that apply)

- A) "abba" → 2
- B) "a" → 1
- C) "abcabcbb" → 3
- D) "" → 0

A: **B) "a" → 1 and C) "abcabcbb" → 3**

'a' returns 0 and 'abcabcbb' returns 2 with these bugs. Surprise: 'abba' returns the right answer (2) because the two bugs cancel out — but after you fix only the length bug it returns 3, so it is still a must-have test. Lesson: one passing test proves little. Empty string passes either way.

cards.heading: The workflow
cards.body: Understand the problem → write a precise prompt → read what comes back → review it line by line → test the edge cases. Never accept AI output you have not run or traced.

packs.title: English · Read-aloud passages
packs.summary: Eight short business passages for pace, pauses and clear stress.

cards.heading: The method
cards.body: The AI scores clarity, pace and completeness. Read at a steady, slightly slower than natural pace, pause at commas and full stops, and never go back to fix a slip — continue.

cards.heading: Passage 1
cards.body: Cloud computing allows companies to rent computing power instead of buying expensive servers. This model, often called pay as you go, helps businesses scale quickly during busy periods and reduce costs when demand falls. However, organisations must still manage security carefully, because data stored in the cloud remains their responsibility.

cards.heading: Passage 2
cards.body: Artificial intelligence tools can now write code, summarise documents and answer questions within seconds. While these tools improve productivity, experts recommend that every output be reviewed by a person. AI systems sometimes produce confident answers that are incorrect, a problem commonly known as hallucination.

cards.heading: Passage 3
cards.body: Agile teams deliver software in short cycles called sprints. At the end of each sprint, the team demonstrates working features to stakeholders and collects feedback. This approach allows requirements to change without derailing the entire project, which is why many enterprises have moved away from traditional waterfall planning.

cards.heading: Passage 4
cards.body: Good communication is one of the most valuable skills for a software engineer. Engineers regularly explain technical decisions to clients who may not share their background. Clear emails, structured updates and active listening help build trust and prevent costly misunderstandings during a project.

cards.heading: Passage 5
cards.body: Cybersecurity threats are increasing every year. Attackers often target people rather than systems, sending convincing emails that trick employees into revealing passwords. Multi factor authentication and regular awareness training are among the simplest and most effective ways to reduce this risk.

cards.heading: Passage 6
cards.body: Before releasing an application, teams run several types of testing. Unit tests check individual functions, integration tests verify that modules work together, and user acceptance testing confirms that the product meets the client's needs. Skipping any of these stages increases the chance of defects reaching customers.

cards.heading: Passage 7
cards.body: Many companies are adopting a hybrid work model, combining days in the office with days at home. Employees value the flexibility, while managers appreciate in person collaboration for planning and problem solving. The challenge is to keep remote and office employees equally informed and included.

cards.heading: Passage 8
cards.body: Data is often described as the new oil, but raw data has little value on its own. It must be cleaned, organised and analysed before it can support business decisions. This is why data engineers and analysts have become essential members of modern technology teams.

cards.heading: Before you move on
cards.body: Record yourself once. Listen for: swallowed word endings, flat pitch, and rushing the last line. Fix one thing per attempt.

packs.title: English · Speak for 60 seconds
packs.summary: Twenty-five speaking prompts and the PREP frame that fits 60–90 seconds.

cards.heading: The PREP frame
cards.body: **P**oint — answer in one sentence. **R**eason — why. **E**xample — one concrete case. **P**oint — restate it. That is 60–90 seconds, and it never leaves you stuck for words.

packs.title: Email · Production outage update
packs.summary: A writing-round email: draft it yourself, then compare with a model answer.

cards.heading: The scenario
cards.body: You are a support engineer. The client's payment service was down this morning (10:05–11:20 IST) due to a failed database migration. Write an email to the client (Mr. Rao) that: (1) explains what happened, (2) states the impact and what was done, (3) gives the plan to prevent recurrence, and (4) proposes a short call tomorrow.

cards.heading: The scoring checklist
cards.body:
- Specific subject line
- Formal greeting
- Explains cause
- Impact / time window
- Action taken
- Prevention plan
- Apology
- Call to action with time
- Professional closing

cards.heading: Your turn
cards.body:
Q: Write the email (about 120 words) before you reveal the model answer.

A: ```
Subject: Payment service outage on 7 October – root cause and next steps

Dear Mr. Rao,

I am writing to update you on this morning's payment service outage.

Between 10:05 and 11:20 IST, customers were unable to complete payments because a database migration failed during a scheduled update. Our team rolled back the change, restored the service at 11:20, and reconciled all affected transactions; no payment data was lost.

To prevent a recurrence, we will run migrations in a staging environment that mirrors production, add an automated rollback check, and schedule future changes outside business hours.

Could we have a 15-minute call tomorrow at 11:00 am to walk you through the full incident report?

We sincerely apologise for the inconvenience and appreciate your patience.

Best regards,
Paikhomba Wahengbam
Support Engineer, Capgemini
```

cards.heading: To remember
cards.body: Specific subject line, formal greeting, cause → impact → action → prevention, one clear call to action with a time, and a professional closing.

```
Steps to reproduce:
```

packs.title: Capgemini 2027 · the exam at a glance
packs.summary: The reported stages, formats and timings — and where that information comes from.

cards.heading: The process, in order
cards.body: As candidates report it: English Communication → Technical Module → Debugging Assessment → AI-Assisted Coding → Cognitive Assessment → Technical + HR interview.

cards.heading: Stage by stage
cards.body:
- **English Communication (LSRW, AI-proctored)** — Read aloud, repeat, sentence builds, speak on topic, grammar, reading, writing/email (~30 min)
- **Technical Module** — 40 MCQs = 20 AI Literacy + 20 Technical (logic/pseudocode, DSA, OOP/DBMS/SQL/Git, cloud/APIs/security) (~40–50 min)
- **Debugging Assessment** — 1 broken program in C / C++ / Java (trees, graphs, 2D DP reported) (~20 min)
- **AI-Assisted Coding** — Solve by directing an AI; graded on prompt quality, approach, review & validation (~45 min)
- **Cognitive Assessment** — Motion Challenge, Grid Challenge, Logical Reasoning, Behavioural (~20–30 min)
- **Technical + HR interview** — Projects/architecture, CS fundamentals, DSA, system design, values (20–35 / 10–20 min)

cards.heading: Where this comes from
cards.body: Source: candidate-reported 2027 pattern (Tech6Sense, TechKalaA, FacePrep, GitHub prep repos, Aug–Sep 2026). Capgemini hasn't published it officially. Super Dream/Alpha-track (~₹13–16 LPA) drives were reported with React-based AI-assisted debugging, AI feature development and a prompt-engineering stage — this plan covers both. 2026 used pseudocode MCQs + 2 coding questions + random games; don't rely only on old papers.

cards.heading: How to use it
cards.body: Every stage above has its own lessons and drills in the 60-day schedule. Check the exam date and format against your own invitation as soon as you have it, and edit the exam milestone in Calendar if it differs.
